name: Proto-Austronesian
notes: Inventory follows the ACD orthography (Blust et al. 2023) used in the source, ch. 3 (p. 49); phonetic values are Shibata's reconstruction (Table 6.13, p. 150). Blust's c, D, ñ and r are left out: the source finds them not well supported by Formosan languages and found in very few PAn reconstructions (pp. 5, 49). It argues against D, c and ñ on pp. 30-33; r gets no argument of its own (p. 49 n. 3 refers to Liao 2024). Blust (2013: 553-591), the Blust system: Table 8.18 (p. 554) has 25 consonants and four vowels; the diphthongs *-ay, *-aw, *-uy, *-iw are listed as sequences, not phonemes. Canonical shape CVCVC or CVCCVC, with clusters only in reduplicated monosyllables and no medial prenasalisation (p. 554). Blust rejects contrastive stress (pp. 554-563), *T (p. 567), *ʔ (pp. 567-574), *b1/*b2 (pp. 574-575), *d1-*d3 (p. 577), *Z (pp. 577-578) and subscripted *R (pp. 588-589), and leaves the evidence for *-ey and *-ew unexplained (pp. 590-591). Higher subgrouping not entered as nodes: Ross (2012) has Puyuma, Tsou and Rukai as first-order branches beside Nuclear Austronesian; Sagart (2004: 421-431; 2026) builds a nested tree on numeral innovations (Pituish, Walu-Siwaish and so on), with Pazeh, Saisiyat and Luilang outside Pituish and Malayo-Polynesian a low-level Formosan subgroup. Wolff (2009: 115-125) argues for a single PAn laryngeal *h (Zorc’s *H) and no *ʔ. Blust & Chen (2017) reject Nuclear Austronesian (Ross) and Ergative Austronesian (Starosta) as resting on negative syntactic evidence.

name: Proto-Atayal
notes: Reconstruction of Goderich (2020: ch. 4), from seven dialects; Shibata (2025: section 3.1) relays it with Li (1981). Its PAn correspondences (Table 4.46, pp. 142-146) are entered from Goderich directly; rows where Shibata's reading differs are cited to Li (1981), whom Shibata relays (decision atayal-original), via Shibata, with Goderich's reading in the notes. Goderich's subgrouping (Figure 6.1, p. 193): Northern Atayal (Matu’uwal; Nuclear Northern: Squliq, Skikun) and Southern Atayal (Plngawan; Nuclear Southern: Klesan; Southwestern: S’uli, Matu’aw), the same tree as Glottolog 5.4. Proto-Atayalic (Li 1981), the ancestor of Proto-Atayal and Proto-Seediq, is not entered as a node (decision atayalic-node). Li (1985: 260) puts Atayalic in his Northern group with Saisiyat, Pazeh and the four north-western plains languages (overlap group).

name: Proto-Seediq
notes: Preliminary reconstruction by the source from Li (1981) and Ogawa & Asai (1935) (section 3.2). Song (2025: 66-67) reconstructs Proto-Seediq independently from five dialects (18 consonants with *c, *x, *h and fricative *g, no *ʔ); it is entered as the reconstruction system “Song”, and the dialects are stated against it (decision song-seediq). Li (1985: 260) puts Atayalic in his Northern group with Saisiyat, Pazeh and the four north-western plains languages (overlap group).

name: Kavalan
notes: The PatRungan (Hsinshe) dialect of Hualien, as described by Li & Tsuchida (2006: 2-11), read directly. Tseng (2022) bases his Kavalan inventory on it (Table 3.1.1, p. 29). Rows from Proto-Kavalan are Tseng’s (Tables 3.2.1, 3.3.1); the older PAn-level rows of Li & Tsuchida, Shibata and Blust were restated against Proto-Kavalan or moved to Proto-Northeast Formosan (decision tseng-nef).
inherit_note: Unchanged: the PatRungan reflex of Tables 3.2.1 and 3.3.1 (pp. 37, 57).

name: Proto-Amis-Sakizaya
notes: Reconstruction of Lin (2022: 56-57), read directly: 16 consonants and four vowels. Shibata (2025: 73) calls the node Proto-Amis and reinterprets two of its phonemes: Lin’s fricative *z as a stop *d, and Lin’s stop *d as *ɮ (n. 14). Since 24 November 2026 the inventory has Shibata’s values, here and in Lin’s lower proto-languages, with Lin’s in the notes of those phonemes and in source_form (decision lin-amis). Lin’s subgrouping (fig. 6.1, p. 112): Proto-Sakizaya (Sakul, Maibul) against Proto-Amis, which splits into Proto-Northern Amis, Proto-Meso Amis and Proto-Tavalong-Fata’an Amis (decision lin-amis). Li & Tsuchida (2022: 96-97) give PAN > Proto-Amis correspondences from the survey of twenty villages that Tsuchida made in 1980. Their Proto-Amis includes Sakizaya, so the rows are entered here, in Lin’s symbols (their r = z, l = ɾ, c = t͡s, q = ʡ, h = ħ). They find no regular sound change that sets any dialect group apart (p. 97) and group the dialects by lexical and sporadic innovations: North (Sakizaya with Northern and Tavalong-Vata’an) against South (Central and Southern) in fig. 1 (p. 107), or Sakizaya split off first in fig. 2 (p. 110), which matches Lin’s tree. Their groups are overlap groups (decision litsuchida-amis).

name: Proto-Bunun
notes: Reconstruction after Li (1988), as given in the source (section 3.3). Li & Zeitoun (2024a: 28): three dialect groups, Takituduh and Takibakha (North), Takbanuaz and Takivatan (Central) and Isbukun; only the Northern dialects keep PB *c and *s apart. Li (1988) read directly in the reprint (Li 2004: 743-766): inventory p. 744, PAN > PB pp. 753-755. His PAN *ʔ (> PB *ʔ) and Tsuchida’s *H (> ø) have no counterpart in the canonical PAN and are not entered. His classification (pp. 756-757): Isbukun split off first; Takituduh and Takibakha keep PB *c and *s apart; Takbanuað and Takivatan share an unexplained final -q in five interrogatives. Li’s own groups are not nodes. Shibata (2020), read directly, reconstructs the same sixteen consonants and three vowels (Table 4.1, p. 62; he writes *b, *d for Li’s preglottalised stops and takes them to be implosives, p. 38), with six diphthongs *ai, *ia, *au, *ua, *iu, *ui (Table 4.13, p. 71) and no word-final *b or *d (§4.3); his PAN > PB rows (pp. 71-79) are entered beside Li’s. He divides the dialects into Northern, Central and Southern (Isbukun) Bunun (fig. 6.1, pp. 113-127); the first two are entered as Proto-Northern and Proto-Central Bunun (decision shibata-bunun-nodes). Blust (1996: 274) gives ‘Bunun’ reflexes of PAN from mixed dialects; his rows are entered here.

name: Thao
notes: Phonology and reflexes after Blust (2003), as summarized in the source (section 3.4). Li & Zeitoun (2024b: 4-5) give 18 consonants and 3 vowels; ʔb, ʔd, l, ʔ and h came in through extensive borrowing from Bunun but are now distinct phonemes. Blust (1996): the vocabulary that Thao shares with Bunun comes from heavy borrowing from Bunun, not from a common ancestor; b, d, l, ŋ, ʔ and h are loan phonemes, found in about 30% of bases (p. 274). On lexical innovations, and on the merger of *n and *ŋ, *l > r and the loss of final glides, Thao groups with the extinct western plains languages, most closely with Taokas and Favorlang-Babuza (pp. 279-281). Blust's labiodental f is entered as ɸ, after Shibata (2025: 59-60) and Li (1976) (decision thao-f).

name: Saisiyat
notes: Examples and reflexes are from the Taai dialect data of Li (1978) (section 3.5). Blust (1999: 45): Northwest Formosan (Saisiyat, Kulon-Pazeh), by the shifts *C > s and *q > ʔ (the node Northwest Formosan here). Li (1985: 260, 271): with Pazeh, the SP branch of his North-western group, by PAN *g' (Dahl’s *j) > z. Hsieh (2007: 11-16), on the modern Taai dialect: 16 consonants p t k ʔ m n ŋ h s (θ) ʃ b [β] z (ð) r l w j and six vowels i œ ə o æ a; the voiced flap (Li’s L, here ɾ) is lost, leaving lengthened final vowels, and Li’s word-internal length before a lost flap is gone (pp. 12-15).

name: Pazeh-Kaxabu
region: Western plains of Taiwan; Puli basin
notes: Language node with no rows of its own (Glottolog’s Pazeh-Kahabu): its dialects Pazeh (Auran) and Kaxabu carry the data.

name: Tsou
notes: Language node with no rows of its own: its entry opens the representative Duhtu dialect (duht1237), which carries Tsuchida’s data; Tfuya is listed beside it. Glottolog’s other dialects, Iimutsu, Luhtu and Tapangu, are not entered (Tung 1964 describes Tapangu, Tfuya and Luhtu; see Tfuya).

name: Kanakanavu
notes: After Tsuchida (1976), as given in the source (section 3.10). Zeitoun (2024a: 4-6, 12) gives 12 consonants and 6 vowels (e and o from monophthongization), three loan phonemes, and the PAN reflexes after the work of Li, and of Tsuchida (1976); fewer than 10 fluent speakers (p. 2). Zeitoun & Teng (2016: 193-195), from voice and nominalization, place Saaroa and Kanakanavu at different levels between PAn and Proto-Nuclear Austronesian (fig. 5), while granting that the phonological and lexical evidence of Tsuchida (1976) favours a Kanakanavu-Saaroa subgroup. Ross (2012) counts both as Nuclear Austronesian. Tsuchida (1975: 27-29), read directly: 13 consonants (h rare, in interjections, loans and as a by-form of s) and four vowels i, ə [ɨ], a, u; o and e only in loans, f only in exclamations (decision tsuchida-1975).

name: Saaroa
region: Central and southern mountains of Taiwan
notes: Correspondences after Tsuchida (1976), as given by Shibata (2025, section 3.11). Inventory after Tsuchida (1976), as given by Shibata (2025: 83-84) (decision saaroa-inventory-pan). Pan (2012: 21-32), on Lha’alua as spoken by the oldest speakers, has the same 13 native consonants and four vowels with /v/ (labiodental; [β] before u in rapid speech) for Tsuchida's β, and the loan phonemes pʰ tʰ kʰ t͡sʰ b ɡ h t͡ɕ d͡ʑ ɛ ɔ (§2.1.4); her allophones are entered. Zeitoun & Teng (2016: 193-195), from voice and nominalization, place Saaroa and Kanakanavu at different levels between PAn and Proto-Nuclear Austronesian (fig. 5), while granting that the phonological and lexical evidence of Tsuchida (1976) favours a Kanakanavu-Saaroa subgroup. Ross (2012) counts both as Nuclear Austronesian. Tsuchida (1975: 59-60), read directly, gives 13 consonants p t c k ʔ s ɬ v m n ŋ l [ɾ] r and four vowels i ə a u, with c [t͡ʃ], ǰ, g, h, o and e in loans.

name: Proto-Rukai
notes: Reconstruction after Li (1977), with the source's changes (section 3.12). Zeitoun (2024b: 3-4) divides Rukai into Maga and Tona on the one hand and Tanan, Labuan, Mantauran and Budai on the other; the six dialects are entered directly under Proto-Rukai, with no subgroup nodes. Li (1977) read directly in the reprint (Li 2004): inventory p. 566 (also p. 593), PAN > PR pp. 588-591, PR > Tanan, Budai, Maga, Tona and Mantauran pp. 582-585 (Labuan is not in his study). His tree (p. 592): Rukai > MTM (MT: Maga, Tona; and Mantauran) and BT (Budai, Tanan); he does not rule out Mantauran as a third branch (p. 593). The groups are not entered as nodes. A first-order branch of PAn in Ross (2012: 1258-1271). Tu (1994: abstract) reaches Li’s grouping from mutual intelligibility: Maga and Tona closest, then Tanan and Budai; Mantauran joins Maga-Tona, remotely.

name: Proto-Puyuma
notes: Reconstruction of Yeh (2024: 137-138), read directly: 18 consonants, four vowels and the diphthongs *aw, *aj, *uj. Yeh’s subgrouping (fig. 6.1, p. 194): Nanwang (with Apapulu) against Proto-Nuclear Puyuma, which splits into Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek (Alripay, Pinaski; Mulivelivek, Danadanaw), Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw and Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan. These nodes are entered (decision yeh-puyuma-tree). A first-order branch of PAn in Ross (2012: 1258-1271).

name: Proto-Paiwan
notes: Reconstruction of Chuang (2024: 52-53), read directly: 22 consonants (*C and *Z with their place left open) and four vowels, from sixteen dialects. Chuang classifies the dialects with a linkage model rather than a tree (ch. 5, fig. 5.1, p. 104): Northern Paiwan Linkage (with a Paridrayan-Tjukuvulj Linkage), Kavulungan Diffusion Area and South-eastern Paiwan Linkage (with a Pacavalj-Tjuabar Linkage); the linkages are nodes of the tree with no proto-language (decision tree-nodes); the Kavulungan Diffusion Area stays an overlap group. Shibata (2025: 94-96) uses Chuang’s reconstruction with his own symbols t͡s, ɖ͡ʐ and s~ʂ.

name: Proto-Malayo-Polynesian
notes: Protophonemes as listed in Table 1.4 of Ross et al. (2023: 30), which shows PAn only for reference. The table has no PMP reflex for PAn h. Blust (2013: 591): PMP shares the problems of PAN reconstruction apart from *C, *N and *S, and unlike PAN permitted medial prenasalisation of obstruents (pp. 591-592).

name: Proto-Oceanic
orthography_note: Orthography of Ross (1988, 1989) with pʷ and kʷ added (Table 1.3, p. 27).
notes: Parent is PMP: the source rejects the interstages PEMP and PCEMP (pp. 40-46). It also argues that early POc kept a third, prenasalised obstruent series (ᵐb, ⁿd, ᵑg; also ⁿr, ñj) from PMP nasal + obstruent clusters, merged with the voiced series in POc as conventionally reconstructed (pp. 33-39), and reports a proposal by Lynch (2022) to revise the vowels (pp. 39-40). Neither revision is in the inventory entered here.

name: Proto-Micronesian
orthography_note: Orthography of Jackson (1986) with s for his d and S for his z, and with y and Z added; ŋ for the velar nasal, ñ for the palatal nasal, superscript ʷ for the labiovelars (Bender et al. 2003a: 2-3).
notes: Consonants from the PMc rows of Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5). The pages entered give no vowel inventory (vowel correspondences are referred to Jackson 1983: 321-323 and Goodenough 1992); the five vowels are those used in the vowel tables of Blumenfeld (2022b: 711-712). In Bender et al. PMc is the ancestor of Kosraean, Kiribati, Marshallese and the Pohnpeic and Chuukic languages (Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6)); Blumenfeld (2022b: 687), following Hughes (2020a, b), adds Nauruan. The Glottolog node Micronesian (micr1243) includes Nauruan. Rehg (1993: 37-40) reconstructs the prosody of PMc: primary stress on the penultimate mora of a phrase (the penultimate syllable of …VCV, the final syllable of …CVV) and high pitch on the antepenultimate mora, with low pitch on the rest, so that stress and high pitch fall on different morae; phrases were minimally trimoraic, a bimoraic noun or verb standing alone being lengthened in its first vowel; and final short high vowels devoiced after a nasal before pause. PMc had 'the same five (short and long) vowels' as Proto-Polynesian (p. 26); the long vowels are not entered (decision rehg1993-pmc).

name: Kosraean
orthography_note: Consonants and glides in IPA, from the phonetic notation of Lee (1975: 4-6, 18-28): orthographic sr is ʂ, r is ɻ (an approximant after Lee & Wang 1984: 436, n. 4; Lee describes a flap), y is j; velarised consonants (Lee's prime, spelled with a following w) are written with ˠ, and rounded ones (Lee's double prime, spelled with o before e and ac) with ʷ; Lee's velarised w' is written w. Bender et al. (2003a) keep Lee's orthographic sr and r; their rows are converted. Vowels: the rewriting by Bender et al. (2003a: 3, Table 1) of the digraph vowels of Lee (1976): ih → ɨ, uc → ə, ac → ε, uh → ʌ, oh → ɔ, ah → æ, oa → ɒ. This matches Lee's own phonetic values (1975: 4, 16), except that the inventory writes the IPA letter ɛ and that Lee describes oa as a low back vowel whose first part is round and last part is not (p. 15).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc; parent_id is therefore PMc and the position in the tree is kept in subgroup_path. A primary branch of PMc in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data source: Lee (1976). Ross et al. (2023: 625, Appendix B.7): Kosraean, glottocode kosr1238, ISO kos, 5.31 162.98. Inventory from Lee (1975: 16, 18-28): consonants in plain, velarised and rounded series (Table 1, p. 18), five glides (p. 26) and twelve vowels, all but the low vowels occurring short or long (p. 16). Lee & Wang (1984) state about 100 cognates against POC in the orthography of Grace (1969); their consonant and vowel reflexes are entered against PMc by composing them with the POc > PMc rows of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5) and, for the vowels, PMc's five vowels taken as POc's unchanged; each row's notes give the POC statement as printed. The velarised and rounded consonants are entered as reflexes of the same PMc consonants as the plain ones, before e and ɛ, where Lee & Wang (1984: 403-404, 415-416) find them distinctive. Not entered from Lee & Wang: POC *q (written *ʔ) > ∅ (p. 407) and *R > ∅ (p. 412), since the database has no PMc reflex of POc *q and POc *R was lost in PMc under unclear conditions; the loss of POC final consonants (p. 413), which PMc had already lost; and the many reflexes of *a that the source does not condition (pp. 421-425). In a postscript Wang suspects direct and indirect inheritance in Kosraean, as in Rotuman (p. 434).

name: Proto-Central Micronesian
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc; parent_id is therefore PMc and the position in the tree is kept in subgroup_path. Following Jackson (1983), the ancestor of Kiribati and all Micronesian languages lower in the tree of Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6) (p. 2).
inherit_note: Not mentioned: Bender et al. (2003) tabulate the consonants only; the vowels of Proto-Micronesian are taken as retained.

name: Kiribati
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Blevins & Harrison (1999: 205-206): standard orthography b [p], bw [pʷ], ng [ŋ], mw [mʷ], r an alveolar tap [ɾ], w [βʷ]. The rows of Bender et al. (2003a), in their comparative transcription (b, bʷ, r, w), were respelled to IPA on 24 November 2026, their letters in source_form.
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PCMc, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Branches from PCMc in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data source: Bingham (1908). Ross et al. (2023: 625, Appendix B.7): Kiribati, glottocode gilb1244, ISO gil, 0.18 173.64.

name: Proto-Western Micronesian
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PCMc, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. The ancestor of Marshallese and all languages lower in the tree of Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6) (p. 2).
inherit_note: Not mentioned: Bender et al. (2003) tabulate the consonants only; the vowels of Proto-Micronesian are taken as retained.

name: Marshallese
orthography_note: Symbols are those of the comparative transcription of Bender et al. (2003a: 2-3), not IPA. Phonemic transcription of Abo et al. (1976) with bʷ for b, mʷ for m̧, ŋ for g, kʷ for q, and superscript ʷ for the rounding of ņʷ, ŋʷ, ļʷ, rʷ (p. 3).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PWMc, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Branches from PWMc in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data source: Abo et al. (1976). Ross et al. (2023: 626, Appendix B.7): Marshallese, glottocode mars1254, ISO mah, 8.72 167.73.

name: Proto-Pohnpeic-Chuukic
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PWMc, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Immediate ancestor of Proto-Pohnpeic and Proto-Chuukic (p. 1); the link to PPON is dashed in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). PMc *x is kept as *x here and splits in Proto-Pohnpeic (decision mc-unchained-cells).
inherit_note: Not mentioned: Bender et al. (2003) tabulate the consonants only; the vowels of Proto-Micronesian are taken as retained.

name: Proto-Pohnpeic
orthography_note: Symbols are those of the comparative transcription of Bender et al. (2003a: 2-3), not IPA. d is a voiceless apico-dental stop (Table 3, note 10); ε is the lax mid front vowel and ɔ the lax mid back rounded vowel written oa (p. 3).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PPC, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Ancestor of Pohnpeian and Mokilese in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6), with Pingelapese to be added (p. 2). Geminate obstruents are realized as homorganic nasal-obstruent clusters in the Pohnpeic languages (Table 2, note 9). The split of PMc *x into r and ∅ is placed here, and PPC *ñ is kept as *ñ (decision mc-unchained-cells).
inherit_note: Not mentioned: Bender et al. (2003) tabulate the consonants only; the vowels of Proto-Micronesian are taken as retained.

name: Pohnpeian
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Rehg (1984: 282-283; Main dialect). Rows from Bender et al. (2003a) were respelled on 24 November 2026, their letters kept in source_form: d (voiceless apico-dental stop, Table 3, note 10) is t; t (lamino-alveolar stop in Bender et al.; Rehg's retroflex affricate, written t with a subscript comma) is ʈ͡ʂ. In Bender et al.'s transcription ε is the lax mid front vowel and ɔ the lax mid back rounded vowel written oa (p. 3).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PPON, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Under PPON in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data sources: Rehg & Sohl (1979); Sohl, Rehg & Andreas (forthcoming). Ross et al. (2023: 627, Appendix B.7): Ponapean, glottocode pona1249, ISO pon, 7.25 158.27. The glottocode printed there is that of the Glottolog dialect Ponapean (pona1249) under Pohnpeian (pohn1238). PPON *ñ is lost (decision mc-unchained-cells).

name: Mokilese
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Harrison (1984: 339). Rows from Bender et al. (2003a) were respelled on 24 November 2026, their letters kept in source_form: d (voiceless apico-dental stop, Table 3, note 10) is t; j (Harrison: 'a prepalatal stop or affricate') is c; the glide y is j. Mokilese e and ε are both written e in Bender et al. (p. 3).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PPON, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Under PPON in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data source: Harrison & Albert (1977). Ross et al. (2023: 626, Appendix B.7): Mokilese, glottocode moki1238, ISO mkj, 6.66 159.78.

name: Pingelapese
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Good & Welley (1989: 2-6): d = t, ng = ŋ, pw = pʷ, mw = mʷ, ae = ɛ, oa = ɔ, h after a vowel for length. The rows of Bender et al. (2003a) were entered in IPA from their comparative transcription (d = t).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PPON, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Not shown in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6); to be included with Pohnpeian and Mokilese (p. 2). Data source: Bender et al. (1984). Ross et al. (2023: 627, Appendix B.7): Pingelapese, glottocode ping1243, ISO pif, 6.21 160.71.

name: Proto-Chuukic
orthography_note: Orthography of Jackson (1983) with y added (p. 3).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PPC, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Figure 1 places tentative or dashed intermediate nodes under PCK (PWCK, PSCK, PNCK, PCCK, PECK); none of them has a row in the tables. Sources: Jackson (1983), Marck (1994). PPC *x is lost (decision mc-unchained-cells). Jackson's (1983: 231) Figure 4 branches off Ulithian first, then Pulo Anna, then Woleaian, then Carolinian-Satawalese, then Puluwatese from Mortlockese-Trukese. The nodes that Glottolog also has (Nuclear, Central and Eastern Trukic, Satawalese-Carolinian, Mortlockese-Trukese) are groups of the tree; his node of everything but Ulithian is not, since Glottolog puts Ulithian with Sonsorol-Tobi in Western Trukic (west2855), and Jackson gives another tree on p. 286 (decision jackson1983-tree).

Jackson & Marck (1991): the Tanapag (Enne) dialect is written with d (p. 148), g (for southern gh, p. 187), h (for southern s, p. 211), rh (for southern sch, p. 381) and n (for southern l, pp. xx-xxi); Ellis (2012: 9) lists the same differences (n : l, rh : sch, h : s) and calls the speech Talaabog, descended mainly from Namonuito settlers (pp. 8-13).

name: Carolinian
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Ellis (2012: 152-153): bʷ, mʷ, pʷː for his labialized-velarized bʷˠ, mʷˠ, pʷˠː; ʈ͡ʂː for his ʈʂ͡:ʲ (decision ellis2012-symbols). Standard spelling (Jackson & Marck 1991: xvii, 27): a á e é i o ó u ú = ɐ æ e ɵ i o ɒ u ʉ; bw = bʷ, pw = pʷː (doubled bw), gh = x, ng = ŋ, sch = ʂ, tch = ʈ͡ʂː (doubled sch), y = j; doubled letters for long vowels and geminates; b, d, g, z in loans. The rows of Bender et al. (2003a), in their comparative transcription, already write these consonants as IPA.
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. (2023: 624, Appendix B.7): Carolinian, glottocode caro1242, ISO cal, 15.21 145.77. Ellis (2012: 8-13) and Jackson & Marck (1991: xv, xx-xxi) describe three dialects on Saipan: the majority southern Elle (EL, *l and *n merged as l), Elle-Enne (LN, l and n kept apart, spoken by people of Tanapag heritage in the south) and Enne, the Tanapag dialect. This lect is the southern speech (EL) of Ellis's inventory; Ellis treats Tanapag (Talaabog) as a separate language close to Namonuito (pp. 10-13; decision jacksonmarck1991-dialects). He finds the consonants of Southern Saipan Carolinian closest to Woleaian (Lamotrekese) and its vowels and lexicon closest to Puluwatese (pp. vi, 156-163).

name: Sonsorolese
orthography_note: Symbols are those of the comparative transcription of Bender et al. (2003a: 2-3), not IPA. á, é, ó, ú are the low front unrounded, mid central unrounded, low back rounded and high central vowels of the Chuukic languages.
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc. The rows are restated here against the immediate ancestor, PCK, by composing the table's rows; each row's notes give the statement against PMc as printed. Not shown in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6); to be positioned on a par with Pulo-Annan (p. 2). Glottolog lists Sonsorolese as a dialect of Sonsorol (sons1242, ISO 639-3 sov). The glottocode and ISO code printed there are those of the Glottolog language Sonsorol (sons1242); Sonsorolese (sons1243) is its dialect. Vita & Pedro (2021: 35-43) re-examine van den Berg's analysis: seven vowels, ə phonemic; short final vowels ɨ̆ ʉ̆ ŏ ɐ̆; diphthongs ɛi ou ɛo ɐɛ ɐʉ ɐo; 16 consonants with ʝ for the palatal and ɣɬ for gl, n not phonemic (it arises from two taps); geminates mː sː ŋː kː fː tː, with pː only in some forms. Their proposed alphabet (Table 6, p. 43) marks long vowels and geminates with a macron (ā, m̄), central and final vowels with a circumflex (â, ê, î, û) and long central vowels with an umlaut (ü), with pw, bw, mw, ng, h (x), r, y (ʝ), d (ð), ghl (ɣɬ) (decision vitapedro2021-phonemes).

name: Nauruan
orthography_note: No standardized orthography: several near-standards are in use (Kayser's grammar, the Nauruan Bible, the 1930s Nauruan language commission, the dictionary draft of Jacob et al. 1996, an informal online system), which differ e.g. in the velar nasal (ṅ, ñ, ng) and above all in the vowels (Blumenfeld 2022a: 653). Blumenfeld (2022a) gives forms in the Jacob et al. spelling beside a transcription: p = pʷ, p; b = bʷ, b; t; d; k; g = ɡ; q = kʷ; m = mʷ, m; n; ñ = ŋ; j; w = w, u̯; r = r, ř; ts (sometimes ds) for the affricate allophones of t, d; i = i, ɨ, i̯, j; e = e, ʌ; a = ɑ, æ; ã = e, i̯e; o = o, ʌ, u̯; õ = ʌ, ɑ, o, u̯; u and ũ = u, ɨ. The two labial series are told apart only by the spelling of the following vowel, the two rhotics not at all (pp. 673, 675-676). The forms behind the correspondences are surface forms in transcription; stress, the allophonic change t, d > ts, dz before i, and gemination of sonorants are not shown (Blumenfeld 2022b: 689).
notes: Treated as a Micronesian language descending from PMc, following Hughes (2020a, b); Jackson (1986) had excluded it from nuclear Micronesian (Blumenfeld 2022b: 687). It shares the merger of *s and *S with all Micronesian languages except Kosraean, but the source calls conclusions about subgrouping premature (pp. 687, 717). Fewer than 200 items are given etymologies and many changes are not fully regular (p. 686). A large layer of Kiribati loans (2022b section 3, pp. 713-717) is entered as loan-stratum rows: voiced ɡ, d for KIR k, t, n for *l in all environments, and ř for KIR r from *s, *S (and from *c, where the inherited reflex is ř as well). Loans usually take the noun prefix dʌ-, do- instead of e- and tend to keep final vowels; old loans have lost them and share other Nauruan changes (pp. 713-714). The inventory follows Blumenfeld (2022a): six long vowels i e æ u o ɑ and two short central vowels ɨ ʌ, which do not attract stress and surface as [u, o] before w and as [i, e] between front consonants (pp. 659, 665, 669-670); the semivowels i̯, u̯ are non-syllabic counterparts of i, u (p. 661; 2022b: 684); m, mʷ, n, r, ř have a singleton-geminate contrast (pp. 653, 657). Hughes (2020b) analyses the affricates before i as phonemes and ʌ, ɑ as allophones (2022a: 672-675). Ross et al. (2023: 626, Appendix B.7): Nauruan, glottocode naur1243, ISO nau, -0.53 166.94.

name: Proto-Coastal Formosan
orthography_note: PAn (ACD) symbols: the source writes its few reconstructions at this level (EF-MP puki, SadiRi, p. 23) in PAn orthography and gives no inventory.
notes: Working hypothesis of Chen et al. (2022): the common ancestor of East Formosan and Malayo-Polynesian, one of nine primary branches of Austronesian (Figures 2, 9 and 11; pp. 4, 20, 22). The evidence is morphosyntactic (transitive use of ma-) and lexical; the only sound change assigned to it is the merger of PAn C and t (Figure 9). The other rows are retentions implied by Figure 9. Neither PMP nor Proto-East Formosan hangs from it here: both are under PAN, and list this node in alt_parents (decision pmp-parent, confirmed 21 November 2026).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Figure 9 (p. 20) of Chen et al. (2022) assigns this node no change to this phoneme.

name: Proto-East Formosan
notes: East Formosan as Glottolog 5.4 has it (East Formosan, east2493: Central East Formosan, Northern East Formosan and Sirayaic), entered under PAN at the user's request (decision pmp-parent, 21 November 2026). Blust's (1999) East Formosan, defined by the merger of PAn j and n, which all its languages accompany with the merger of PAn C and t; Blust posits that merger three times independently, in Proto-East Formosan, in Bunun and in PMP (Blust 1999: 46, quoted in Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 12). Li & Zeitoun (2024a: 13) also list loss of PAn q among Blust's East Formosan mergers; it is not entered, since Proto-Amis has ʡ for PAn q (Lin 2022). Chen et al. (2022: 12, 20) make it a sister of Malayo-Polynesian under Proto-Coastal Formosan (Figure 9; alt_parents); Sagart (2004, 2014) disputes the subgroup (Chen et al. 2022: 13). Glottolog's Northern East Formosan (Kavalan, Basay, Ketangalan; Tseng's 2022 Proto-Northern East Formosan) is not entered as a node. Blust (1999), read directly: Table 3 (p. 45) lists for East Formosan the mergers of *t/C and *j/n and the shift *q > ʔ; for its Northern branch (Basay-Trobiawan, Kavalan) the merger of *q with zero (presumably through *ʔ, p. 46), the merger of *n (from *j and *n) with *N, and *susu > *sisu ‘breast’.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Figure 9 (p. 20) of Chen et al. (2022) assigns this node no change to this phoneme.

name: Siraya
notes: Not spoken since the early twentieth century (Adelaar 2011: 2, cited in Shibata 2025: 98); left out of the source's main discussion because the surviving transcriptions are inconsistent and the cognates few (pp. 98-99). Two dialects are cited, that of the Gospel translations and that of the Utrecht Manuscripts (Adelaar 1999, 2014; pp. 17, 103-104, 107 n. 15). Adelaar (2014) reconstructs Proto-Siraya ð and d for the PAn voiced coronal obstruents (p. 98); his Proto-Siraya and its dialects are entered from Adelaar (2014) itself as the lects psiraya, siraya-g and siraya-um. Blust (1999a) puts Siraya with Kavalan, Amis and Basay in East Formosan on the merger of j and n; the source does not adopt the subgroup (pp. 7, 163). Entered under Proto-East Formosan (decision pmp-parent). Adelaar’s (2014: 9-10) dialect reflexes of PAn *d (Gospel r, d root-initially; Utrecht Manuscript s, d in clusters) are entered on the two dialects themselves, against Proto-Siraya *ð (p. 10), and not here.

name: Basay
notes: Entered for Samtiau New (Shinshe), the dialect on which Li (2014) and Tseng (2022: 67-68) base the Basay inventory; recorded by Asai in 1936 (p. 6). Extinct. Older rows that spoke of Basay in general were restated against Proto-Basay or moved to Proto-Northeast Formosan (decision tseng-nef).
inherit_note: Unchanged: the Samtiau New reflex of Tables 4.2.1 and 4.3.1 (pp. 72, 86).

name: Taokas
notes: One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which the source leaves out of its main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). The source treats Taokas as a language; it is listed under Babuza, as in Glottolog. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN. Li (2003: 942-944) groups Taokas, Babuza, Papora and Hoanya as the Northwestern subgroup (the node Central Western Plains here), with Taokas and Babuza closest (after Tsuchida 1982: 10) and Papora close to them; Thao is more distantly related to the four and Pazih more distant still (tree, p. 948). Blust (1999: 45) puts it in his Central Western Plains, under Western Plains. Li (1985: 260) puts it in the TBPH branch of his North-western group, within the Northern group (overlap groups).

name: Babuza
notes: Language node with no rows of its own (Glottolog’s Babuza: Favorlang, Poavosa and Taokas): the dialects carry the data. Li (2003: 99 n. 5) and Li (2005: 181) take Favorlang to be an earlier form of Babuza.

Li (2003: 942-944) groups Taokas, Babuza, Papora and Hoanya as the Northwestern subgroup (the node Central Western Plains here), with Taokas and Babuza closest (after Tsuchida 1982: 10) and Papora close to them; Thao is more distantly related to the four and Pazih more distant still (tree, p. 948). Blust (1999: 45) puts it in his Central Western Plains, under Western Plains. Li (1985: 260) puts it in the TBPH branch of his North-western group, within the Northern group (overlap groups). The source treats Papora as a language; it is listed under Papora-Hoanya, as in Glottolog.

Li (2003: 942-944) groups Taokas, Babuza, Papora and Hoanya as the Northwestern subgroup (the node Central Western Plains here), with Taokas and Babuza closest (after Tsuchida 1982: 10) and Papora close to them; Thao is more distantly related to the four and Pazih more distant still (tree, p. 948). The source treats Hoanya as a language; it is listed under Papora-Hoanya, as in Glottolog.

name: Ketagalan
notes: Named only in a passage translated from Ogawa (1931: 35-36), in quotation marks (p. 14); the source says nothing more about the language or about what Ogawa's label covers. Ketangalan is Glottolog's name. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7). Entered under Proto-Northeast Formosan, Glottolog’s Northern East Formosan; Tseng (2022: 4-5) follows Ogawa in treating Basay and Ketangalan as one language (decision tseng-nef).

name: Kaxabu
region: Western plains of Taiwan; Puli basin
notes: The second dialect of Pazeh-Kaxabu, spoken in four villages of Puli Township; data mostly from Lim's fieldwork since 2014 (Lim & Zeitoun 2024: 330-332). Li & Tsuchida (2001: 2) call it less conservative than Auran Pazeh (the lect entered as Pazeh). Kaxabu has lost the flap r (Pazeh r < PAN *l), merged final l with n, turned Pazeh ħ into a glottal h, and developed e and o (from final au and lowering before h) (pp. 334-335).

name: Proto-Celebic
orthography_note: j continues PMP z by an orthographic convention of the source (PMP *z = PCEL *j, p. 311); y continues PMP j and y; ə is PMP e (schwa); e and o are the vowels from PMP -ay and -aw.
notes: Tentative reconstruction by the source, based on Mead's (2003) six innovations (pp. 300, 311; fn. 6); reflexes from the PCEL column of Table 18 (p. 312) and sections 2 and 4.1. Not entered as rows: medial clusters C1C2 > C2 where C1 was not a nasal (Mead's innovation 1, p. 300); nasal clusters mp, mb, nt, nd, ns, ŋk are kept (Table 18). PCEL kept (almost) the full range of PMP final consonants (p. 314). The source's Celebic is Tominic, Kaili–Wolio and Eastern Celebic (Saluan–Banggai, Bungku–Tolaki, Muna–Buton), without Badaic and Rampi (pp. 299, 301). No inventory is given; this one is generated from the reflexes.

name: Proto-Kaili–Wolio
region: Central Sulawesi; homeland placed around Lake Poso (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny). å is a vowel found only word-finally, from *a/*ə + *R.
notes: Reconstructed by the source. Vowel inventory stated in section 4.1 (p. 303); the consonants are those of the PKW column of Table 18 (p. 312), which is a table of non-final reflexes and not an inventory, plus d and g from the reconstructions. The only final consonant reconstructed is ʔ; the source leaves open whether PKW kept more final stops or final nasals (pp. 314-315). Daughters allow only NC clusters medially (p. 314).

name: Proto-Northern Kaili–Wolio
region: Central Sulawesi; homeland placed between Tentena and Poso (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny).
notes: Northern branch: Greater Kaili (Common Kaili, Sedoa, Kulawi, Lindu), Topoiyo, Uma, Pamona (p. 302). The source gives PNKW forms throughout the appendix but no inventory; it is generated from the reflexes. Most of Martens's (1997) Proto-Kaili–Pamona reconstructions can be taken as PNKW (p. 303); the appendix cites them next to the PNKW forms. No glottocode: Glottolog's Northern Kaili-Wolio includes Ledo, which the source puts in the Southern branch.

name: Proto-Southern Kaili–Wolio
region: Sulawesi; dispersal placed in the Wotu area (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny).
notes: Southern branch: Ledo (dominant lexical stratum), Wotu, and Island Kaili–Wolio (Wolio, Kamaru, Kalao, Loa') (p. 302). PSKW forms are given in the appendix but no inventory; it is generated from the reflexes. Not entered as rows: an added w in two etyma, PKW *uaʔ > PSKW *uwa 'vein' and *ue > *uwe 'water' (Table 23, p. 316). No glottocode: Glottolog's Southern Kaili-Wolio does not include Ledo.

name: Wolio
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Southern Kaili–Wolio > Island Kaili–Wolio
orthography_note: The source writes the implosive /ɓ/ as b throughout (fn. 26); entered here as ɓ.

name: Proto-Sumatran
region: Sumatra and the Barrier Islands off its west coast
orthography_note: The source's symbols: ɡ (IPA g), ə for the schwa (PMP e), y for the palatal glide.
notes: Reconstructed by the source from seven pre- and proto-languages (Pre-Gayo, Proto-Batak, Proto-Northern BI, Proto-Central BI, Pre-Mentawai, Pre-Enggano, Pre-Nasal) as a branch of PMP defined by five mergers and one shift (Table 31, p. 133): *j, *ɡ > *ɡ; *z, *d > *d; *R, *r > *r; *ñ, *n > *n; *h > Ø; *q > *h. Inventory from Table 12 (p. 125). Besides the inventory, homorganic nasal-stop sequences (*mb, *nd, *ŋɡ, *mp, *nt, *ŋk) and *rC sequences are reconstructed word-medially, and the vowel sequences *au and *ua; *uə and *əu are only marginally attested (pp. 130, 132). *y is not word-initial; *ə is not found in open word-final syllables (p. 132). PMP *c is not considered: no inherited reflex is attested by several Sumatran languages (pp. 137-138). The Glottolog node Sumatran (suma1277) follows this paper and has the same seven branches.

name: Pre-Gayo
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Gayo varieties (Bukit, Cik, Dëret, Lues, Serbejadi), from Hazeu (1907), Eades (2005) and Shorto (1976) (section 2.1, pp. 117-118). Inventory from Table 1 (p. 117); also the nasal-stop sequences *mp, *nt, *ŋk. *b, *d, *ɡ are not reconstructed although Hazeu's dictionary has many examples, likely borrowed (pp. 117, 137); /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). The correspondence tables write Pre-G *e (Table 26) and *o (Table 29), which are not in Table 1 (ɛ, ə, ɔ); they are entered as printed. Irregular forms shared with Proto-Batak (not entered as rows): *aɡi > *aŋɡi (Pre-G *əŋɡi), and an added final *h in *waluh 'eight' and *siwah 'nine' (p. 141). No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Gayo (gayo1244) is entered separately.

name: Gayo
notes: The source states two correspondence sets among the Gayo varieties (pp. 117-118): the diphthongs of the Lues variety against the mid vowels of Bukit and Dëret, and the 'funny' (post-ploded) nasals, kept apart from plain voiced stops mainly by older speakers (Eades 2005). They are entered here with the variety or generation in the environment; the remaining Pre-Gayo phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the source names only two correspondence sets among the Gayo varieties, the diphthongs and the funny nasals (pp. 117-118).

name: Proto-Batak
notes: Simplified overview following primarily Adelaar (1981) (section 2.2, pp. 118-119). Inventory from Table 2 (p. 118); also *mb, *nd, *ŋɡ, *mp, *nt, *ŋk and *rC sequences between vowels. *c and *j are not word-final, *y is not word-initial. *j is [dʒ] (fn. 4). The source gives no PSUM origin for PB *c and *j: claimed reflexes of PMP *c have no cognates in the other Sumatran languages (pp. 137-138), and /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). Glottolog's Batakic (toba1265) also has Alas-Kluet, which the source does not name (it speaks of 'at least seven' Batak languages and lists six).

name: Proto-Northern Barrier Islands
region: Pulau Simeulue and Pulau Banyak, Aceh
notes: Ancestor of Haloban, Leukon and Simeulue (section 2.3, pp. 120-121). Also the sequences *mb, *nd, *mp, *nt, *ŋk between vowels. *b and *d are not word-final; *r, *w, *y, *ʔ are not word-initial; *p occurs only word-finally and between vowels after *ə. The status of final *s is unclear (fn. 26, p. 151). Finer vowel developments in the NBI languages are left aside by the source (p. 150). /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). No glottocode: Glottolog has Haloban and Leukon as dialects of the language Simeulue (sime1241), not as a family.

name: Proto-Central Barrier Islands
notes: Ancestor of Sigulai and Nias (section 2.4, pp. 121-122). Inventory from Table 6 (p. 121). No word-final consonants and no word-final diphthongs; the medial sequences *mb and *nd (not *ŋɡ) are reconstructed. *ʔ, *x, *r, *y are not word-initial. An adjacent PSUM *r, itself lost, changed the vowels: *a, *ə, *u > *o and *i > *e, in the vowel next to initial or final *r, in the leftmost of two identical vowels, or in the vowel lowest on the hierarchy i > u > a > ə of two unlike vowels; *ara > *o (p. 130). Excrescent nasals in single words (fn. 33-35, pp. 152-153) are not entered. Same membership as Glottolog's Nias-Sikule (nias1241).

name: Pre-Mentawai
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Mentawai varieties, from Pampus (1989, 1994), Lenggang (1992) and Morris (1900) (section 2.5, pp. 122-123). Inventory from Table 8 (p. 122); nasal-stop sequences are also reconstructed. Voiced stops are not word-final, *j is only medial, *k and *s are not word-final. The correspondence tables also give Pre-M *w (from final *ɡ and *k, forming a diphthong with a preceding *a or *ə, p. 126) and *uy (Table 30), which are not in Table 8; they are entered as printed. No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Mentawai (ment1249) is entered separately.

name: Mentawai
notes: A group of diverse varieties. The source states four nontrivial correspondence sets among them without a table (p. 123): final nasals and final voiceless stops (kept apart in some varieties, merged as stops or as nasals in others), geminate stops against nasal-stop sequences (the nasal assimilates fully to the stop in some varieties; not entered as rows, the clusters are not listed), and initial d against r. The merger of *s and *t as t in the Simalegi variety is from p. 143. The remaining Pre-Mentawai phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the source names only four nontrivial correspondence sets among the Mentawai varieties (p. 123).

name: Pre-Enggano
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Enggano dialects, from the data up to Kähler (1987), largely after Edwards (2015) (section 2.6, pp. 123-124). Inventory from Table 9 (p. 123). No coda consonants and no word-final diphthongs. Nasality is a word-level feature: PSUM coda nasals, and final *l and *r (after *i) through a merger with *n, made the word nasal unless *ə preceded, and were then lost; the nasals themselves became *b, *d and (through *ɡ) *h. A '~' in the source's tables marks a reflex in a nasal word; it is given in the notes here. The source orders the changes in three stages (Table 39, pp. 138-140): 1. *b, *p > *p; *s, *t > *t; loss of *h; changes of *r; *k > *ʔ. 2. *w > *b; *t > *k; suprasegmentalisation of nasality. 3. *ɡ > *h; loss of codas. Edwards (2015) reconstructs *t where the source has *d for the d/r : t set (p. 124). No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Enggano (engg1245) is entered separately.

name: Enggano
notes: Old Enggano: the language up to and including Kähler's (1987) dictionary. The two columns of Table 10 (p. 124), South and West, are the dialects of that period; they are entered with the dialect in the environment. Later changes (Yoder 2014, Edwards 2015: erosion of final vowels, split of /o/ into /o/ and /ɘ/; p. 140) are not entered. The remaining Pre-Enggano phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 10 (p. 124).

name: Pre-Nasal
notes: Reconstruction for Nasal, which has no known dialect differences; based on the authors' documentation (McDonnell 2017a, b, 2019) and earlier wordlists (section 2.7, pp. 124-125). Inventory from Table 11 (p. 125). *b, *d, *ɡ are not word-final and *y is not word-initial; *o (from *a) and *ʔ (contrasting with *k) are only word-final. The voiced obstruents are kept next to *ə and in nasal-stop sequences; elsewhere *b > *w, *d > *χ, *ɡ > *h, and word-finally they are devoiced. Most other b, d, ɡ of modern Nasal are borrowed, and /r/ for PMP *j is attributed to Lampungic loans (pp. 125, 137); /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). Nasal gives no clear evidence for or against the merger of *ñ and *n (pp. 134-135). No separate lect is entered for modern Nasal: the source states no change after Pre-N.

Clark writes PNCV *R where an etymon keeps *R in some NCV languages and loses it in others, and *r where all NCV languages keep it; all non-zero reflexes of *R in NCV are identical with those of *r (p. 149). Root-final *R is lost with all word-final consonants, a late change in the history of the linkage (p. 151). François finds that *R-loss spread word by word from the south: for each etymon the languages keeping *R lie north of the isogloss and those losing it south of it (pp. 155-156, 166-168, 15 isoglosses). name: Proto-New Caledonian

Vowels are not reconstructed there. Geraghty (1989) calls the same node Proto-Southern Oceanic (New Caledonia and the Loyalties); his changes are rows citing him (decision nc1992-geraghty). Forms are also cited by François (2011: 170), who modifies an earlier reconstruction: *p not yet lenited and diphthongs not yet monophthongized (fn. 36). The New Caledonian languages are Grande Terre and the Loyalty Islands (fn. 5); they are in the Southern Oceanic linkage with Vanuatu. Glottocode newc1243 (New Caledonian).

name: Proto-Kajang
notes: Sekapan, Kejaman and Lahanan (Smith 2017a: 93-99; Figure 23, p. 97). The fricative *ɮ from *l in the onset of the final syllable is 'unique in all of Borneo' (p. 95). The internal subgrouping is unresolved (pp. 96-97). Smith finds no evidence for a Melanau-Kajang node (pp. 106-111, Figure 26), so Kajang and Melanau are entered separately under PMP. Figure 23 also has *CC > *ʔC (clusters from the loss of a middle vowel in three-syllable words, p. 96), not entered as a row. Glottolog's Kajang (kaja1255) has the same members. Under Proto-Central Sarawak (Smith 2023: 361-362; decision smith2023-nodes).

Smith thinks it 'likely' that final high vowels had become *əw and *əy in Proto-Melanau (p. 103); nothing else is assigned to it. Glottolog's Melanau (mela1255) has the same members. name: Proto-Punan
notes: Punan Tubu, Punan Bah, Punan Aput, Beketan, Ukit and others (Smith 2017a: 111-127; Figure 27, p. 112). 'Proto-Punan had not undergone any major changes'; the subgroup rests on lexical innovations, above all the metathesis *təlaʔus > *təlasuʔ 'barking deer' (p. 114). Smith treats Punan as one language with dialects (p. 120). His internal split into Punan Tubu-Bah and the rest (Figures 28-29, pp. 122-124) has conflicting evidence (p. 122), so no lower nodes are entered; the changes are entered on each lect. Table 31 has '?' for PMP *r. Glottolog's Punan (puna1280) follows Smith's grouping. Under Proto-Central Sarawak (Smith 2023: 361-362; decision smith2023-nodes).
inherit_note: Unchanged from PMP in Table 31 (p. 114), which sets PMP and Proto-Punan side by side.

name: Proto-Müller-Schwaner

His internal subgrouping has three primary branches (Upper Mahakam, Kereho, Hovongan; Figure 38, p. 139), so no lower nodes are entered. Table 39 has '?' for PMP *r. Glottolog's Muller-Schwaner (mull1247) has the same members. Under Proto-Central Sarawak (Smith 2023: 361-362; decision smith2023-nodes).

name: Proto-Polynesian
notes: Inventory: Table 2.1 (p. 22) and §3.1 (p. 73). Tongic and Nuclear Polynesian are the primary split (p. 25; Figure 1.2, p. 3). Under Proto-Central Pacific, with Geraghty's (1986) PCP > PPn rows (decision geraghty1986-ppn, reverted by the user on 23 November 2026). Marck doubts the PPn *s/*h distinction (Table 2.2 note 5, p. 24) but keeps it, as does Wilson (2021: 44). The tree below follows Wilson (2021: 42) (decision pn-tree); Marck's (2000) and Walworth's (2014) parents are proposed parents.

name: Proto-Tongic
notes: Tongan and Niuean (Figure 1.2, p. 3). PPn *s and *h fell together as *h and *r was lost (p. 25).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.

name: Proto-Nuclear Polynesian
notes: All Polynesian languages other than Tongic (p. 118). PPn *r merged with *l and *h was lost (p. 25). East Uvean, East Futunan, Pukapukan and the 'Futunic' Outliers are unclassified Nuclear Polynesian (§5.5, p. 128).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.

name: Proto-Ellicean
notes: Samoan, Ellicean Outlier and East Polynesian (§5.6, p. 129; Figure 1.2, p. 3); defined by three sporadic vowel changes and no consonant change (p. 129); first proposed on the evidence of pronominal systems. Glottolog's Ellicean (elli1239) is Pukapuka, Samoan-Tokelauan and Tuvalu, a different group, so no glottocode. Wilson (2021: 43) no longer accepts the group. Marck's (2000) node. In the main tree the Polynesian lects follow Wilson (2021) (decision pn-tree); Marck's daughters that Wilson places elsewhere are its proposed daughters, and its changes are composed onto them.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.

name: Proto-Ellicean Outlier
notes: Tuvalu, Tokelauan and the Central and Northern Outliers, as in Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24). Marck calls the evidence for the group weak: one shared sporadic vowel change (§5.7, pp. 129-130). Tokelauan shares sporadic changes with Samoan (§5.8, pp. 130-131; decision tok-placement). Marck's (2000) node. In the main tree the Polynesian lects follow Wilson (2021) (decision pn-tree); Marck's daughters that Wilson places elsewhere are its proposed daughters, and its changes are composed onto them.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.

Parent after Wilson (2021); Marck's (2000) parent, Proto-Ellicean, is a proposed parent (decision pn-tree).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.
