name: Proto-North Sarawak
orthography_note: Blust writes PNS schwa ə where PMP has *e (2007: 6-7), and the voiced aspirates bʰ dʰ jʰ gʰ.
notes: Kelabitic, Kenyah, Berawan-Lower Baram and Bintulu (Blust 2007: 7, Table 3; 2002: 384). Its defining innovation is the split of the PMP voiced obstruents into plain voiced stops and voiced aspirates (Blust 2007: 7). Entered under PMP from Blust's Table 2, although decision smith-higher-order holds Smith's North Sarawak back (decision pns-node). Glottolog's North Sarawakan (nort3171) has the same members.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 2 (Blust 2007: 6) gives the same symbol for PNS.

name: Proto-Kenyah
notes: Highland and Lowland Kenyah, the latter including Sebop and Penan (Blust 2007: 6, Figure 1). PK kept the PNS voiced aspirates as a distinct series (p. 7) and had a six-vowel system, adding *e and *o by lowering before final *h from *R and *s (p. 10). Glottolog's Kenyahic (keny1280) has Kenyah, Sebop and Penan.
inherit_note: Not among the changes that 'distinguish Proto-Kenyah from PNS' (Blust 2007: 7): retained.

name: Chamorro
orthography_note: Topping's spelling as Blust (2000: 84-85) uses it: ' glottal stop, ch [ts], y [dz] (Blust respells final -ai, -ao, -ui as -ay, -aw, -uy), ñ, ng, gw. Low front æ is not written in the dictionary; Blust marks it as ([æ]).
notes: Mariana Islands. Blust (2000) states its reflexes against PMP (p. 88) and finds no subgroup between the two: Chamorro is a primary branch of Malayo-Polynesian with no close relatives (§4, pp. 103-104). Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4.

name: Palauan
orthography_note: Blust's phonemicization (2009: 308): y and w are glides, written i/e and u/o in the standard orthography; ð is written d, ʔ ch, ŋ ng.
notes: Palau. With Chamorro one of the two non-Oceanic Austronesian languages of the Pacific (Blust 2000: 83); Blust (2009) states its reflexes against PMP (Table 2, p. 309) and gives it no closer relatives. Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4.

name: Òma Lóngh
orthography_note: Soriente's spelling (Blust 2007: 8-9): é è ó ò are tense and lax mid vowels, e is both [ə] and [ɯ] (from *u), j is [ɟ] (unreleased [c] finally), f [ɸ], v [β], gh [ɣ], ngh a voiceless velar nasal. Blust writes ʔ for Soriente's apostrophe.
notes: Upper Malinau and upper Pujungan rivers, East Kalimantan; about 3,000 speakers, long isolated from other Kenyah (Blust 2007: 8). A Highland Kenyah language (p. 10); Blust derives it from Proto-Kenyah. Data from Soriente (2006). Glottolog 5.4: Uma' Lung, under Highland Kenyah (Upper Pujungan).

name: Kiput
orthography_note: Blust's spelling (2002: 385): e is schwa, é a mid front vowel, ë a mid-central glide in falling diphthongs, c a voiceless palatal affricate, ʔ the glottal stop; I and U are lax vowels of loanwords. Final -ey, -ew are written -ei-, -eu- before a final consonant.
notes: One longhouse (Long Kiput) on the Baram River, Sarawak; about 450 speakers. Berawan-Lower Baram branch of North Sarawak (Blust 2002: 384). Blust derives it directly from PNS (p. 385); Lower Baram and Berawan-Lower Baram nodes are not entered. Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4 (North Sarawakan > Berawan-Lower Baram > Lower Baram > Central Lower Baram A).
inherit_note: Unchanged: 'It will be assumed that no change has taken place unless stated otherwise' (Blust 2002: 423), in the summary of shifts, splits and mergers.

name: South Efate
orthography_note: Lynch writes South Efate phonemically (2000b: 321): ᵏp and ᵑm are labiovelars (IPA k͡p, ŋ͡m here), ⁿr a prenasalised trill; long vowels are written double. Final POc V or VC is generally lost and nouns often carry the accreted article n(a)- (written na/ here as in the source).
notes: Language node with no rows of its own: its entry opens the representative Erakor dialect, which carries Lynch's (2000b) data; Eton and Epau, with the reflexes Lynch reports from Clark (1985), are listed beside it (decision sef-dialects).

name: Naman
orthography_note: Lynch's orthography (2019b: 22), mainly Crowley's: j = /c/ [tʃ], ns = /j/ [ntʃ] ~ [ns], x = /ɣ/, ŋ, ə, and long vowels written double; b d g are prenasalised and r is a flap. Entered in IPA (decision lynch-ipa). na/, ne/ etc. mark the accreted article *na.
notes: Moribund Western Malakula linkage language (Southwestern group), now spoken by a score of adults in Litzlitz and nearby villages on the east coast; formerly spoken further west in north-central Malakula (Lynch 2019b: 21). Data from Crowley (2006a). Lynch states its reflexes against POc, citing PEOc, PRemote Oceanic, PSOc and PNCV forms where POc has none; entered under POc (decision lynch-parents). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626).

name: Nese
orthography_note: Lynch's orthography (2019c: 62), after Crowley and Takau: linguolabials written with a following apostrophe (b', v', m'), j = /c/, r = flap, rr = trill; x for their kh and ŋ for ng. Entered in IPA (decision lynch-ipa). na/, ne/ etc. mark the accreted article *na.
notes: Moribund Northern Malakula language of the Matanvat area, northwest Malakula, actively spoken by fewer than five people; with Botovro, Vovo and Vao it forms the North Coast subgroup, and with Malua Bay the Northern subgroup (Lynch 2019c: 61, Figure 1). Data from Crowley (2006b) and Takau (2016). Lynch states its reflexes against POc, citing PEOc, PRemote Oceanic, PSOc and PNCV forms where POc has none; entered under POc (decision lynch-parents). *d, *r, *dr and retained *R merge as rr, an innovation shared by the whole Northern subgroup (p. 68). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626), which gives no ISO code.

name: Proto-Batanic
notes: Yami, Itbayat, Ivatan and Babuyan (Ross 2005: 2-3; Yang 2002). Ross: Batanic is Malayo-Polynesian but shares no innovation with any other Philippine group, and apart from PMP *R > *y 'very little phonological change has occurred' (pp. 12-15). Yang reconstructs Proto-Batanic from Tsuchida et al.'s (1987) data (ch. 4) with 19 consonants and four vowels (Table 4-1, p. 43); his tree (p. 65) separates Itbayat (keeps *h, loses *q) from Yami-Ivatan-Babuyan, and Yami from Ivatan-Babuyan (*l1 > d, *r > l), without intermediate reconstructions (decision yang-tree). Yang's Proto-Batanic keeps *R apart from *y (decision pb-r). Glottolog's Batanic (bata1315) has the same members.

name: Yami
orthography_note: Yang follows Tsuchida et al. (1987): z is the alveolar trill r, r the retroflex fricative ʐ, d a retroflex stop ɖ, s a voiceless retroflex fricative ʂ, h a voiced uvular fricative ʁ, N ŋ, c j the palatal affricates t͡ʃ d͡ʒ, e a schwa (Yang 2002: 15-16; decision yang-ipa). Glottal stop is not a phoneme in Tsuchida's analysis.
notes: Lanyu (Orchid Island), Taiwan; dialects Imurud, Iraralay, Iranumilek (Ross 2005: 2). Yang lists 11 changes (§5.2.1, pp. 46-51). Unstressed vowels are centralised to ə. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog. Yang's (2002: 65) tree puts Yami with Ivatan and Babuyan against Itbayat (*q > h, loss of *h), and then apart from Ivatan-Babuyan (*l1 > d, *r > l). Glottolog instead groups Yami with Itbayat (Yami-Itbayat, yami1257). He reconstructs no intermediate languages, so none are nodes (decision yang-tree).
inherit_note: Table 5-1 (p. 64) lists every consonant; the vowels stayed largely the same (pp. 40-42).

name: Itbayat
orthography_note: Yang follows Tsuchida et al. (1987): x is a voiced uvular fricative ʁ, M ɲ, N ŋ, ? ʔ, c j t͡ʃ d͡ʒ, e a schwa, o a high vowel (Yang 2002: 16-17; decision yang-ipa).
notes: Itbayat Island. Often treated as a dialect of Ivatan (Ross 2005: 3). Yang lists 10 changes (§5.2.2, pp. 51-54); /f/ occurs only in loans (p. 45). Glottolog names ivat1242 'Itbayat'. Yang's (2002: 65) tree separates Itbayat first from Yami-Ivatan-Babuyan: Itbayat keeps *h and loses *q, where the others have *q > h and lose *h. He reconstructs no intermediate languages, so none are nodes (decision yang-tree).
inherit_note: Table 5-1 (p. 64) lists every consonant; the vowels stayed largely the same (pp. 40-42).

name: Ivatan
region: Batan and Sabtang Islands, Batanes, Philippines
orthography_note: Yang follows Tsuchida et al. (1987): M ɲ, N ŋ, ? ʔ, c j t͡ʃ d͡ʒ, e a schwa, o a high vowel; vowel length marks penultimate stress (Yang 2002: 17, 46; decision yang-ipa).
notes: Batan and Sabtang; dialects Ivasay and Isamurung (Ross 2005: 2-3). Yang lists 13 changes (§5.2.3, pp. 54-59); /f/ only in loans. Glottolog's ibat1238 (named 'Ibatan', ISO ivb) holds Basco and Southern Ivatan and Babuyan; glottocode and ISO code from Glottolog. Yang's (2002: 65) tree groups Ivatan most closely with Babuyan (*l1 > d, *r > l), then with Yami, and last with Itbayat. He reconstructs no intermediate languages, so none are nodes (decision yang-tree).
inherit_note: Table 5-1 (p. 64) lists every consonant; the vowels stayed largely the same (pp. 40-42).

name: Babuyan
orthography_note: Yang follows Tsuchida et al. (1987): M ɲ, N ŋ, c j t͡ʃ d͡ʒ, e a schwa, o a high vowel; no v, ʔ or x (Yang 2002: 17; decision yang-ipa).
notes: Babuyan Island, repopulated at the end of Spanish rule by Ivatan speakers from Batan; some speakers are bilingual in Ilokano (Ross 2005: 3). Yang treats it as a language and groups it most closely with Ivatan (p. 65); Glottolog has it as a dialect of ibat1238. Yang lists 10 changes (§5.2.4, pp. 59-62). Yang's (2002: 65) tree: Ivatan-Babuyan (*l1 > d, *r > l), then Yami, then Itbayat. He reconstructs no intermediate languages, so none are nodes (decision yang-tree).
inherit_note: Table 5-1 (p. 64) lists every consonant; the vowels stayed largely the same (pp. 40-42).

name: Proto-Northern Luzon
notes: Formerly 'Cordilleran' (Reid 2006: 1). Reid's tree (Figure 1, p. 4) has Altan, Meso-Cordilleran (South-Central Cordilleran), Arta, Ilokano and Northern Cordilleran (Cagayan Valley and Northeastern Luzon; Robinson & Lobel 2013 make Northeastern Luzon a primary branch instead). Two phonological innovations define the group: loss of word-final glottal stop and the metathesis of *t and a following sibilant (pp. 6-7). Reid includes *j in the inventory because of /d/ reflexes in some languages (Table 1, p. 6; Table 2, p. 7); *j otherwise falls together with *ɡ. Ross (2005: 14), citing Reid, adds the loss of PMP *h. Only these rows are entered; the inventory is Reid's Table 2. Glottolog's Northern Luzon (nort3238).

name: Proto-Northeastern Luzon
notes: Dupaningan Agta, Pahanan Agta, Paranan, Dinapigue Agta, Casiguran Agta and Nagtipunan Agta; not Kasiguranin (Robinson & Lobel 2013). Defined by *R > ɡ together with *j > d (pp. 131-134). R&L make it a primary branch of Northern Luzon (p. 125) but state the changes from PMP (decision neluz-parent). Their tree (pp. 147-148): Dupaningan a primary branch; Casiguran with Nagtipunan; Pahanan with Paranan; Dinapigue unplaced (decision neluz-internal). Consonants geminate after ə (R&L 2013: 136; not entered as rows, decision neluz-gemination). Low Vowel Fronting (*a > e after b d ɡ) is sporadic and found in different words in each language (pp. 136-137). Glottolog's Northeastern Luzon (nort3187). Since 24 November 2026 under Proto-Northern Luzon, of which Robinson & Lobel make it a primary branch; their rows, stated against PMP, are restated against Reid's (2006) inventory, except those for PMP *h and *z, which that inventory lacks (decision neluz-parent).

name: Dupaningan Agta
notes: A primary branch of Northeastern Luzon (R&L 2013: 147-148). Data mostly the northern dialect (Robinson 2011), which keeps r and merges ə with a (pp. 153, 155). Consonants geminate after ə (R&L 2013: 136; not entered as rows, decision neluz-gemination). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Pahanan Agta
notes: Groups with Paranan (R&L 2013: 148). Consonants geminate after ə (R&L 2013: 136; not entered as rows, decision neluz-gemination). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Paranan
notes: The non-Agta language of Palanan; groups with Pahanan Agta (R&L 2013: 148). Its Low Vowel Fronting forms are mostly borrowed from Pahanan Agta (p. 137). Consonants geminate after ə (R&L 2013: 136; not entered as rows, decision neluz-gemination). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Dinapigue Agta
notes: Not previously described; one afternoon with one speaker (R&L 2013: 131). Its position inside Northeastern Luzon is unresolved (p. 148). Consonants geminate after ə (R&L 2013: 136; not entered as rows, decision neluz-gemination). No glottocode in Glottolog 5.

name: Casiguran Agta
notes: Groups with Nagtipunan Agta (R&L 2013: 147-148). Casiguran has lost the gemination after ə found in the other languages and does not share sporadic *s > h (pp. 136, 145). Glottolog's Casiguran-Nagtipunan Agta (casi1235) covers both; glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Nagtipunan Agta
notes: Not previously described (R&L 2013: 131); groups with Casiguran Agta, 77 percent similar on a 200-word list (pp. 147-148). Too few data to say whether consonants geminate after ə (p. 136). A dialect of Glottolog's Casiguran-Nagtipunan Agta (casi1235), which has no separate glottocode for it.

name: Proto-Central Luzon
notes: Kapampangan, Sinauna and the Sambalic languages, three equidistant branches (Himes 2012: 527; decision himes-nodes). Himes states the changes from PMP ((2), p. 492). His inventory (3) (p. 493) is p t k ʔ b d z j ɡ s m n ŋ l r w y and i ɨ u a, with ɨ for the PMP schwa; the inventory here is generated from the rows and comes out the same. (2) also lists *j > d, *d > l / V[-back]_V and *z > d, which (3) does not reflect; they are entered on the branches (decision himes-apicals). All the languages except Kapampangan insert ʔ between identical vowels (p. 495); entered on Sinauna and Proto-Sambalic. Himes (§6.2, pp. 530-532) finds Bashiic no closer to Central Luzon than to Cordilleran, though both share *R > y. Glottolog's Central Luzon (cent2080).
inherit_note: Not mentioned among the early changes of (2) (p. 492): retained.

name: Sinauna
region: Tanay, Rizal and Infanta, Quezon, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Data from Santos (1975), with a Remontado list from General Nakar, Quezon (Himes 2012: 491); Himes cites Remontado forms as SIN (REM). Shares only the lowering of ɨ with Kapampangan and no rule with Sambalic (p. 527). Also: *yʔ (< *Rʔ) metathesises to ʔy (*ma-bɨyʔat > mabáʔyat 'heavy', p. 496). Glottolog's Hatang Kayi (Remontado Dumagat, remo1247), of which Sinauna is another name; glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Kapampangan
notes: §2.5 (Himes 2012: 497-500). Kapampangan alone does not insert ʔ between identical vowels: it merges them into one long vowel (*tuud > tud 'knee', p. 499). Like Bashiic it metathesises a word-initial *CɨC- to aCC- (*bɨyas > abyas 'husked rice', p. 531). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Proto-Sambalic
notes: Bolinao, Sambal Tina and Botolan Sambal, with the Ayta languages Mag-antsi, Mag-indi, Ambala and Magbukun, whose speakers first acquired Austronesian from Botolan Sambal speakers (Himes 2012: 512, 527). Changes not shared with Sinauna and Kapampangan (§2.6, pp. 500-509); most of them have different outcomes in each language and are entered on the lects. Himes does not reconstruct lower nodes for phonology (decision himes-nodes). Glottolog's Sambalic (samb1319).

name: Bolinao
region: Bolinao and Anda, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Bolinao and Anda (Himes 2012: 491). The only Sambalic variety whose glottal stop is unchanged (p. 501). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Sambal Tina
region: Santa Cruz to Iba, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Santa Cruz, Candelaria, Masinloc, Palauig and Iba (Himes 2012: 491). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Botolan Sambal
region: Botolan and Cabangan, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Botolan and Cabangan; the Ayta of Villar, Kakilingan and Abellen speak varieties of it that do not differ significantly in phonology (Himes 2012: 491). *ʔl metathesises to lʔ, as in Mag-antsi, Mag-indi and Ambala (*laʔlu > *lalʔu > la:ʔu 'pestle', p. 502). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Mag-antsi Ayta
region: Porac, Pampanga (resettled in Capas, Tarlac), Luzon, Philippines
notes: Data from speakers originally of Cagmang, Porac, resettled after the 1991 Pinatubo eruption (Himes 2012: 491). Himes: the Ayta acquired their Austronesian from Botolan Sambal speakers (pp. 512, 527); Botolan's other changes may hold here too but are entered only where Himes cites this language. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Mag-indi Ayta
notes: Data from Floridablanca, Lumibao and Maague-ague (Himes 2012: 491). Himes: the Ayta acquired their Austronesian from Botolan Sambal speakers (pp. 512, 527); Botolan's other changes may hold here too but are entered only where Himes cites this language. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Ambala Ayta
region: Olongapo and San Marcelino, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Data from Pastolan and Gordon Heights, with two SIL lists (Himes 2012: 491). Himes: the Ayta acquired their Austronesian from Botolan Sambal speakers (pp. 512, 527); Botolan's other changes may hold here too but are entered only where Himes cites this language. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Magbukun Ayta
region: Mariveles and Morong, Bataan, Luzon, Philippines
notes: Data from Biaan (Mariveles) and Canawan (Morong), with SIL lists (Himes 2012: 491). Final *y < *R is not replaced by ʔ (luŋúy 'to hear', p. 500). Himes: the Ayta acquired their Austronesian from Botolan Sambal speakers (pp. 512, 527); Botolan's other changes may hold here too but are entered only where Himes cites this language. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Glottolog.

name: Proto-Northern Atayal
notes: Goderich (2020: §6.2): ancestor of Matu’uwal, Squliq and Skikun, defined by the merger of final *-lit and *-liʔ and by lexical innovations (Table 6.4). Tables 6.1-6.3 give its consonants and vowels.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Goderich's tables of Proto-Atayal reflexes at this node (pp. 194-197) show it unchanged.

name: Proto-Nuclear Northern Atayal
notes: Goderich (2020: §6.2.1): ancestor of Squliq and Skikun. Five shared sound changes (the merger of *ɹ and *y, liquid assimilation, affrication of *t, final *b devoicing, prepenultimate vowel lenition) plus *w fortition (p. 198). The affrication of *t is entered on Squliq and Skikun instead, because in Squliq it followed the merger of *c and *s (p. 119) and in Skikun it applies only before i (p. 124). Word-final *g was still present (p. 199).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Goderich's tables of Proto-Atayal reflexes at this node (pp. 197-201) show it unchanged.

name: Proto-Southern Atayal
notes: Goderich (2020: §6.3): ancestor of Plngawan, Klesan, S’uli and Matu’aw, defined mainly by lexical innovations (Table 6.10) and by the merger of *q and *ʔ and final *b devoicing, which Goderich assumes happened before the split (p. 202). The loss of final *g happened independently in each dialect.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Goderich's tables of Proto-Atayal reflexes at this node (pp. 202-205) show it unchanged.

name: Proto-Nuclear Southern Atayal
notes: Goderich (2020: §6.3.1): ancestor of Klesan, S’uli and Matu’aw. The merger of *ɹ and *y is its only consonant change (independent of the same merger in Nuclear Northern Atayal); vowels unchanged (Table 6.12).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Goderich's tables of Proto-Atayal reflexes at this node (pp. 206-209) show it unchanged.

name: Proto-Southwestern Atayal
notes: Goderich (2020: §6.3.1.1): ancestor of S’uli and Matu’aw; the merger of *c and *s is its only consonant change (Table 6.14), vowels unchanged (Table 6.15). Glottolog 5.4 has no node for S’uli and Matu’aw alone.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Goderich's tables of Proto-Atayal reflexes at this node (pp. 210-212) show it unchanged.

name: Matu’uwal
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Jinshui Village (Caburuk), Miaoli County (Goderich 2020: 13). The Qing’an variety has merged c with s (p. 40). Conservative: no mid vowels in native words (p. 40). Lu (2005: 17-23), also on Mayrinax: 17 consonants (Table 2.1), b realized [β] or [v] ([v] in codas) and g as [ɣ]; three vowels i, u, a, with [e] and [o] only as allophones next to q or h or in loans, and no schwa.
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Squliq
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Data from dictionaries and Goderich's fieldwork (p. 13); the largest dialect. A few I-lan villages have lost q (p. 32). Rau (2000) studies the Squliq of the Mstbon (Ruiyan) community in Nantou, where word-final p, m and l are changing to k, ŋ and n by lexical diffusion; that community is entered as the sub-dialect Mstbon Squliq (mstbon), listed under Squliq. Rau (1992: 18-24), on the Squliq of Wulai, has 19 consonants p b m t r n s c z l k ɡ ŋ x q h ʔ y w and six vowels i e a o u ü, with ü only in a few words (perhaps from Chinese loans) and schwa treated as a transition, not a phoneme; Goderich’s inventory is kept.
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Skikun
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Skikun tribal village, I-lan County (p. 13).
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Plngawan
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Sasi tribal village, Ren’ai Township, Nantou County (pp. 13, 42). The only dialect that keeps *ɹ apart (p. 42).
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Klesan
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Pyahaw tribal village, I-lan County (p. 13), one of five Klesan villages; Ropoy and Kəŋyan keep final l (Li, cited p. 46). A stratum of Squliq loans (§5.5.1).
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: S’uli
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Spoken in Hsinchu, Miaoli and Taichung (p. 37); data from various villages in Hsinchu and Miaoli (p. 13), less than planned because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Matu’aw
orthography_note: Goderich's orthography (Table 1.2): c [t͡s], h [ħ], y [j], b [b~β~v], g [ɡ~ɣ], r [ɾ~r].
notes: Two tribal villages in Ta-hsing Village, Tai’an Township, Miaoli County (p. 51); data less than planned (p. 13). No mid vowels; diphthongs kept (p. 52).
inherit_note: Unchanged: §4.5 lists all regular sound changes from Proto-Atayal to each dialect (p. 116).

name: Proto-Siraya
orthography_note: Adelaar's symbols: ł (probably a palatal lateral), ɣ, ð, y.
notes: Reconstruction of Adelaar (2014), bottom-up from the Gospel (G) and Utrecht Manuscript (UM) dialects of the 17th-century Dutch records, with the later Siraya Proper, Makatau and Taivuan wordlists as circumstantial evidence only (pp. 3-4). PS still distinguished PAn *R (*ɣ) and *S (*s), which merged in every attested dialect (pp. 14-16, 30). Tentative: written evidence only, probably missing a glottal stop and stress (p. 30). Glottolog's Sirayaic (sira1267) has the same members, but that code is held by the lect Siraya, which carries the comparisons of Shibata, Ross and Blust for the language as a whole.

name: Siraya, Gospel dialect
orthography_note: Adelaar's spelling of the Dutch records: x is a voiced palatal fricative (2014: 4 n. 2), D a root-initial d/r.
notes: The dialect of the Siraya translations of the Gospel of St Matthew and the Heidelberg Catechism, printed in 1661 and 1662, the main 17th-century record (Adelaar 2014: 3). Li (2009: 405-407), read directly, takes St Matthew and the Formulary to be based on a Taivuan dialect (*D, *Z > r, d; loss of -k- and -g-; future -ah), with some dialect mixture.

name: Siraya, Utrecht Manuscript dialect
orthography_note: Adelaar's spelling of the Dutch records: x is a voiced palatal fricative (2014: 4 n. 2), D a root-initial d/r.
notes: The dialect of the wordlist and dialogues of the Utrecht Manuscript, published by Van der Vlis in 1842 (Adelaar 2014: 3); based on a Siraya dialect, like the Sinkang and Tohkau manuscripts (s for *D; Li 2009: 405-407).

name: Taivoan
notes: Formerly spoken mostly inland from the Tainan Plain to the north (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 25). Li & Zeitoun take the Dutch Gospel and Catechism of 1661-1662 to be Taivuan. Reflexes from Li (2009: 400-404), read directly, stated against PAn and restated here against Proto-Siraya (Adelaar 2014). Li’s preferred tree, by the order of the changes, splits off Siraya first and groups Taivuan with Makatau (Figure 2, p. 407; overlap group); counting shared changes instead would split off Taivuan first (Figure 1, p. 404).

name: Makatao
notes: Formerly spoken in Kaohsiung and Pingtung (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 25). Reflexes from Li (2009: 400-404), read directly, stated against PAn and restated here against Proto-Siraya (Adelaar 2014). Li’s preferred tree, by the order of the changes, splits off Siraya first and groups Taivuan with Makatau (Figure 2, p. 407; overlap group); counting shared changes instead would split off Taivuan first (Figure 1, p. 404).

name: Tanan
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: Spoken in the east, in Taitung County (p. 2). Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977). Li (1977: 582) states the changes from Proto-Rukai and leaves out what is unchanged (p. 582), so the lect is stated-unchanged after him. Li (1973: 15-16), on Tanan (Taromak), has 22 consonants p b t d T D k ɡ ʔ c s θ ð h v m n ŋ r l L w y (T, D, L retroflex) and four vowels i u ɨ a: p and h, which Zeitoun’s table lacks, and no o ([o] is the commonest variant of /u/, p. 16). Zeitoun’s inventory is kept.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Li leaves out ‘the sounds that remain unchanged’ (p. 582).

name: Labuan
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: Spoken in Pingtung County (p. 2). Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977).

name: Budai
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: Spoken in Pingtung County (p. 2). Table 53.3 lists no p, although Table 53.5 has Bd pito 'seven'. Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977). Chen (2006: 218-232): 20 consonants, including p; vowels i, u, ə, a, with [o] a free allophone of u. Li (1977: 582) states the changes from Proto-Rukai and leaves out what is unchanged (p. 582), so the lect is stated-unchanged after him.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Li leaves out ‘the sounds that remain unchanged’ (p. 582).

name: Maga
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: One of the 'Three Lower Villages' (p. 2). The only dialect with consonant clusters, from the deletion of unstressed vowels (p. 8). Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977). Hsin (2000: 19-35) also gives 18 consonants (ð and z after Li, despite their rarity, no glottal stop, no glides) and seven surface vowels; she argues that e, o and ə are synchronically derived from i, u, ɨ. Li (1977: 583) states the changes from Proto-Rukai and leaves out what is unchanged (p. 582), so the lect is stated-unchanged after him.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Li leaves out ‘the sounds that remain unchanged’ (p. 582).

name: Tona
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: One of the 'Three Lower Villages' (p. 2). Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977). Li (1977: 583-584) states the changes from Proto-Rukai and leaves out what is unchanged (p. 582), so the lect is stated-unchanged after him.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Li leaves out ‘the sounds that remain unchanged’ (p. 582).

name: Mantauran
orthography_note: Zeitoun's IPA; orthography tr, dr, lr, th, dh, c, ng, ’, é, e, ɨ.
notes: One of the 'Three Lower Villages' (p. 2); the most drastic consonant changes (p. 5). Its position has long been disputed; recent studies group it with Tanan, Labuan and Budai (pp. 3-4). Inventory from Tables 53.3-53.4 of Zeitoun (2024b: 7-8); the dialect changes she states (pp. 5-7) are entered against Proto-Rukai (Li 1977). Li (1977: 584-585) states ten changes from Proto-Rukai (entered); the lect is not set to stated-unchanged because he says nothing of PR word-final *w and *y, which the inventory lacks.

name: Nanwang
notes: The dialect described by Teng (2008), 'the most conservative' (p. 5): alone in keeping the voiced stops (Ting 1978). Ting's (1978) Proto Puyuma 'looks almost exactly the same as' Nanwang (p. 5). Yeh (2024: 26-27) finds t, d and l dental (t̪, d̪, l̪) by EMA and ultrasound; the inventory stays Teng’s. Cauquelin (2015: 6-7) adds /ʃ/, the loan phonemes /d͡ʒ/ and /f/, and a marginal /o/.

name: Katipul
notes: One of the six varieties compared by Ting (1978), cited by Teng (2008: 4-5). Ting's subgroup of all dialects except Nanwang (the voiced stops became fricatives) is not entered as a node (decision puyuma-ting). Teng's later work groups Katripul with Kasavakan and Ulivelivek with Tamalakaw, Rikavung, Pinaski and Alipay (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 30). Yeh (2024) writes Katripulr; its ð-ʐ distinction is being lost (pp. 30-31, 161).

name: Rikavung
notes: One of the six varieties compared by Ting (1978), cited by Teng (2008: 4-5). Ting's subgroup of all dialects except Nanwang (the voiced stops became fricatives) is not entered as a node (decision puyuma-ting). Teng's later work groups Katripul with Kasavakan and Ulivelivek with Tamalakaw, Rikavung, Pinaski and Alipay (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 30). Yeh (2024) writes Likavung and separates it from Tamalrakaw on lexical grounds only; the two have the same sound system (pp. 29, 193).

name: Kasavakan
notes: One of the six varieties compared by Ting (1978), cited by Teng (2008: 4-5). Ting's subgroup of all dialects except Nanwang (the voiced stops became fricatives) is not entered as a node (decision puyuma-ting). Teng's later work groups Katripul with Kasavakan and Ulivelivek with Tamalakaw, Rikavung, Pinaski and Alipay (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 30). Yeh (2024): ð and ʐ have merged as ð since Ting’s fieldwork (p. 32).

name: Pinaski
notes: One of the six varieties compared by Ting (1978), cited by Teng (2008: 4-5). Ting's subgroup of all dialects except Nanwang (the voiced stops became fricatives) is not entered as a node (decision puyuma-ting). Teng's later work groups Katripul with Kasavakan and Ulivelivek with Tamalakaw, Rikavung, Pinaski and Alipay (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 30).

name: Ulivelivek
notes: One of the six varieties compared by Ting (1978), cited by Teng (2008: 4-5). Ting's subgroup of all dialects except Nanwang (the voiced stops became fricatives) is not entered as a node (decision puyuma-ting). Teng's later work groups Katripul with Kasavakan and Ulivelivek with Tamalakaw, Rikavung, Pinaski and Alipay (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 30).

name: Saichia
notes: Tjaylaking village, Santimen Township, North Paiwan (Chang 2006: 12-13); keeps tj and dj, as palatalized dentals, so belongs to neither of Ho's groups (Chang 2006: 12).

name: Santi
notes: Stimur village, Santimen (Sandimen) Township, North Paiwan. One lect for three descriptions of the same place (decisions chen-paiwan-dialects, chuang-paiwan-dialects): Chang (2006: 12-13), Ho's Northwestern group, having merged tj and dj with t and d; Chen's (2006) Northern Paiwan (Sandimen, also Majia; pp. 21-22, 47), which has also merged *q with ʔ and *ʎ with l (Table 2.4; some older speakers keep [ʎ], p. 133); and Chuang's (2024: 4-8) Timur (三地門), from a vocabulary handbook by Cheng and a co-author, in his Northern Paiwan Linkage (p. 104). The inventory is Chang's, with the phonemes only Chen or Chuang has added from them; each row and allophone keeps its source. Li & Zeitoun (2024a: 30) put Stimul among the t-merger dialects of Ferrell & Tjakisuvung.

name: Isbukun
notes: The most divergent Bunun dialect; 'it can be hypothesized that Isbukun split off from Proto-Bunun first' (Li & Zeitoun 2024a: 28). Inventory from Li (2018: 27), on the Isbukun of Dongpu village, Nantou. Li (1988: 743-752) gives its reflexes of Proto-Bunun, entered here. Allophonic only, and not entered: *t palatalized as [c] before i (p. 744); v and ð devoiced word-finally, [f] and [θ] (p. 749). Shibata (2020: 80-84, 126-127) puts Isbukun alone in a Southern group (fig. 6.1) and takes its word-final b and d, which Li (1988) took to be retentions, to come from paradigm regularization in verbs: only verbs and nouns with a verbal form keep them, and PAN *d is lost finally in Isbukun too (paniʔ ‘wing’, ikuʔ ‘back’).

name: Tamalrakaw
notes: Puyuma dialect described by Yeh (2024: 29-30, 157), treated by Ting (1978) together with Likavung; Yeh separates the two on lexical grounds (p. 193). Glottolog has no languoid for it.

name: Tfuya
notes: The dialect of Zeitoun’s Tsou chapter (2005b: 260), entered for its inventory (decision tsou-tfuya). Zeitoun treats [w] as non-phonemic and analyses long vowels as sequences of like vowels (p. 261). Glottolog name Tfuea. Li (1979: 214) gives the Tfuya (and Tapangu) reflexes of Duhtu r < PAN *l, entered against PAN *l. Tung (1964: 7, 18-20) describes the Tapangu, Tfuya and Luhtu dialects: 15 consonants p t c k ʔ b d f s h v z m n ŋ (no phonemic y or w) and six vowels i ʉ u e o a; Luhtu may have a further apical vowel where the others have e (pp. 20-21), and Tfuya and Luhtu have clusters with z where Tapangu has i (p. 18).

name: Teruku
notes: The dialect of Tsukida’s Seediq chapter (2005: 291), spoken mainly in Hualien; entered for its inventory, with no correspondences (decision tsou-tfuya).
inherit_note: Inferred: the source gives the inventory only; a phoneme that the inventory shares with the parent is taken as retained (decision tsou-tfuya).

name: Takivatan
notes: Central Bunun in Glottolog (with Takbanuaz). Entered for the inventory of De Busser (2009: 113-130); Li (1988) gives its reflexes of Proto-Bunun, entered here. Shibata (2020) puts it with Takbanuað in Central Bunun (Proto-Central Bunun).
inherit_note: Inferred: the source gives the inventory only; a phoneme that the inventory shares with the parent is taken as retained (decision tsou-tfuya).

name: Central Paiwan
notes: Chen’s (2006) Central Paiwan, described from Piuma village (also Gulou; pp. 21-23); with Southern Paiwan the most conservative variety (p. 313).

name: Southern Paiwan
notes: Chen’s (2006) Southern Paiwan (Shimen, Mudan; pp. 21-22, 48-49).

name: Proto-Sakizaya
notes: Lin (2022: 113-123): retains every PAS phoneme; the subgroup rests on sporadic, morphological and lexical innovations (Tables 6.3-6.5). Glottolog: Sakizaya.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Tables 6.1-6.2 (pp. 113-114) give PS the same reflex as PAS.

name: Proto-Amis
notes: Lin (2022: 123-128). Its one regular change is PAS *z > *r (Table 6.7); sporadic and lexical evidence in Tables 6.9-6.10. Not Shibata’s (2025) Proto-Amis, which is Lin’s Proto-Amis-Sakizaya (pami).
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the changes of Tables 6.6-6.8 (pp. 124-126).

name: Proto-Northern Amis
notes: Lin (2022: 129-131): no sound change; morphological (*<um> > <əm>) and lexical evidence. Glottolog’s Northern Amis.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Tables 6.11-6.12 (pp. 129-130).

name: Proto-Meso Amis
notes: Lin (2022: 131-136): *b > *β and *d > *ɮ (Table 6.14), with sporadic, morphological and lexical evidence. Covers Glottolog’s Central and Southern Amis; no single languoid. The same group as the South (Central and Southern) of Li & Tsuchida (2022: 98-111), which they support by lexical innovations and two sporadic changes: s > h in the instrumental prefix sa- (entered) and l > ʔ in *SuReNa ‘snow, ice’ (soldaʔ > soʔdaʔ, p. 98), not entered because none of Lin’s dialect inventories has a glottal stop.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the changes of Tables 6.14-6.15 (pp. 132-133).

name: Proto-South-Central Amis
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the changes of Tables 6.19-6.20 (p. 137).

name: Proto-Central Amis
notes: Lin (2022: 139-141): Kalala and Kiwit; no regular change, lexical and sporadic evidence (Table 6.24). Narrower than Glottolog’s Central Amis (cent2104), which includes the Coastal dialects such as La’enu, so no glottocode.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Tables 6.22-6.23 (pp. 139-140).

name: Proto-Tavalong-Fata’an Amis
notes: Lin (2022: 141-143): *b > *v (Table 6.25) and *C<um>V > *ʔəmV. Glottolog: Tavalong-Vataan.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the changes of Tables 6.25-6.26 (p. 142).

name: Sakul Sakizaya
notes: Lin (2022: 5, 42); data from Cheng’s vocabulary handbook of the dialect, on which the inventory is based (Lin 2022: 6-7, 42).

name: Proto-Northeast Formosan
notes: Reconstruction of Tseng (2022: 94-119), read directly: the ancestor of Kavalan and Basay, with 16 consonants (Table 5.4.1, p. 119), four vowels and four diphthongs. Tseng posits *Q (the reflex of PAn *q, giving Proto-Kavalan *ʔ and the shift *a > *i next to it) beside *q (from PAn *k next to *ʁ). Subgrouping evidence: the retraction of PAn *k next to *R and the metathesis of *dalan to *razan (pp. 117-118). Glottolog’s Northern East Formosan (Kavalan, Basay, Ketangalan). Kavalan, Basay and Ketagalan were moved here from Proto-East Formosan, and their older rows restated against the new parents (decision tseng-nef). Blust (1999: 45-46): the Northern branch of East Formosan merges *n (from *j and *n) with *N (entered) and *q with zero, presumably through *ʔ (not entered: Tseng’s *Q).

name: Proto-Kavalan

Tseng’s classification (fig. 3.1, p. 65): a Northern Yilan subgroup (*q > χ: Xiblaxuen, Sahut, Xitmixu, XizmamaR, and within it Meso-Northern Yilan, with *ʁ > χ as well: Pali, Sinahan, Xibluwan, Tubi), a Southern Yilan subgroup (metathesis in ‘fire’: Kralut, PatRungan, Nanfang-ao, Xilinaw), and Xitnurikan, XibuRaw and Ximlawlaw on their own. The subgroups are not entered as nodes; the dialects are stated against Proto-Kavalan as in Tables 3.2.1 and 3.3.1 (decision tseng-nef). No glottocode: Glottolog's kava1241 is the language Kavalan, not a clade.

name: Proto-Basay

No glottocode: Glottolog's basa1287 is the language Basay, not a clade.

name: Proto-Atayalic
notes: Reconstruction of Li (1981), read in the reprint (Li 2004), from seven Atayal dialects (Squliq of Pyasan, Maspaziʔ, Skikun, Mnawyan, Mayrinax, Matabalay, Palŋawan) and four Seediq dialects (Toŋan, Toda, Truwan, Inago) (p. 625). Inventory p. 662, with the diphthongs aw, ay, uy; PAN > Proto-Atayalic pp. 662-667. Not the parent of Proto-Atayal and Proto-Seediq here, which stay under PAN (decision atayalic-node) and list it as an alternative parent (decision li-atayalic). Li’s correspondence sets from Proto-Atayalic to the eleven dialects (§2, pp. 633-661) are not entered. Not entered either: PAN *iw > PA *uy (*kaSiw > *kahuy ‘tree’), the exceptions for *k’ and *g, and the intrusive consonants of Atayalic male forms (pp. 666-667). Li (1985: 260) puts Atayalic in his Northern group with Saisiyat, Pazeh and the four north-western plains languages (overlap group).

name: Takituduh
notes: One of the five Bunun dialects of Li (1988). Northern dialect (pp. 743, 756). Inventory after Cheng (2017), as given by Shibata (2020: 38): b and d are implosives. Shibata puts it with Takibakha in Northern Bunun (Proto-Northern Bunun).

name: Takibakha
notes: One of the five Bunun dialects of Li (1988). Northern dialect (pp. 743, 756). Inventory from Jiang (2012: 23-30), on the Takibakha of Dili village: 16 consonants and five vowels. Jiang derives e and o from ai and au (p. 29); Shibata (2020: 45) and Li (1988) take e and o to be realizations of the diphthongs. Jiang’s b and d are [ʔb], [ʔd] between vowels and plain elsewhere (p. 25); Cheng’s Tannan data have implosives (Shibata 2020: 42). Shibata puts it with Takituduh in Northern Bunun.

name: Takbanuað
notes: One of the five Bunun dialects of Li (1988). Central dialect (pp. 743, 756). Spelled Takbanuaz by Li & Zeitoun (2024a). Inventory from Shibata (2020: 46), from his own work with a speaker from Wanhsiang (Kalibuan) village, Nantou: no c, and implosive b, d. Shibata puts it with Takivatan in Central Bunun.

name: Proto-Northern Bunun
notes: Shibata (2020: 113-120): Takituduh and Takibakha, grouped by lexical innovations and shared sporadic changes (Tables 6.2-6.4, pp. 116-120). Its consonants are those of Proto-Bunun (Table 6.1), so it has no regular sound change of its own; Li (1988) grouped the two dialects by their keeping PB *c and *s apart, which Shibata rejects as a retention (p. 114). Glottolog: North Bunun.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Shibata’s Table 6.1 (p. 115) gives every Proto-Bunun consonant unchanged in Proto-Northern Bunun, and the vowels are the same in all dialects (Table 4.12, p. 70).

name: Proto-Central Bunun
notes: Shibata (2020: 120-126): Takbanuað and Takivatan, grouped by the q-final interrogatives first noted by Li (1988) and other lexical innovations (Tables 6.6-6.7). PB *c and *s merge as *s (Table 6.5, p. 121), which Shibata takes to be a change of Proto-Central Bunun itself (p. 126). Glottolog: Central Bunun.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Shibata’s Table 6.5 (p. 121) gives every other Proto-Bunun consonant unchanged in Proto-Central Bunun, and the vowels are the same in all dialects (Table 4.12, p. 70).

name: Umiray Dumaget
notes: Eastern coast of central Luzon and Polillo Island (Lobel 2013: 212). Under Greater Central Philippine after Himes (2002) and Glottolog (decision lobel-umiray). Lobel (§7.9) rejects this membership and lists four possibilities (with Northeastern Luzon, with Central Luzon, with Manide-Alabat, or a separate Philippine branch); his placement directly under PMP is a proposed parent. The rows are restated against PGCPh *ʔ, *ɡ, *d, *ə (composed). Reflexes from Himes (2002: 278-280) as Lobel discusses them. Low Vowel Fronting (*a > [e] after b d g w y) is productive and allophonic in Umiray Dumaget (Lobel 2013: 216, n. 9), so it is not entered.

name: Proto-Manide-Alabat
notes: Lobel's Manide-Alabat subgroup, which 'appear[s] to form a primary branch of the Philippine macrogroup' (2013: 236, 271-275); there is no Proto-Philippine node, so it sits under PMP. Glottolog's Alabat-Manide Agta (alab1255) has the same two members but is placed under Central Philippine. Lobel cites PMA forms (*hidá, *didá, p. 253) but gives no inventory; it is generated from the rows. The /y/ reflex of *l, *-r-, *-d-, *-j-, *-z- is a borrowed stratum from a Central Philippine language (pp. 248-249, 259-265).

name: Manide
notes: Camarines Norte (Lobel 2013: 236-241); Glottolog's 'Camarines Norte Agta'.

name: Inagta Alabat
notes: Alabat Island and Lopez, Quezon (Lobel 2013: 241-242); Glottolog's 'Alabat Island Agta'.

name: Proto-Greater Central Philippine
notes: The node against which Lobel states Proto-Subanen (2013: 303-317). Its PMP > PGCPh changes are only those Lobel mentions (pp. 213-215, 246); its inventory is 'the general Philippine phoneme inventory' (p. 310), including *ʔ (from *q) and *h. Glottocode grea1284 (Greater Central Philippine), although Glottolog also includes Alabat-Manide, which Lobel excludes (decision lobel-pgcph); Umiray Dumaget is under this node after Himes (2002) (decision lobel-umiray).
inherit_note: Not stated by Lobel: taken as unchanged from PMP (Proto-Subanen shows 'no additions to the general Philippine phoneme inventory', p. 310).

name: Proto-Subanen
notes: Defined by five phonological and 74 (70) lexical innovations (Lobel 2013: 304-309). Inventory Table 10.3 (p. 311). Tree Figure 10.1 (p. 308): Western Subanen (Western Subanon, Western Kolibugan) and Nuclear Subanen; Nuclear Subanen has a 'West Nuclear' pair (Tawlet-Kalibugan, Salug-Godod) that keeps *r and an East Nuclear branch with *r > l. *g-addition (§10.4) is an inserted-sound row. Not entered: in reduplicated monosyllables the penult vowel became *ə and the initial consonant was lost or replaced by *g (§10.5).

name: Proto-Western Subanen
notes: Western Subanon and Western Kolibugan (Figure 10.1, p. 308). Their *r > l happened independently of East Nuclear Subanen, probably through contact (p. 308).

name: Proto-Nuclear Subanen
notes: Defined by the sporadic loss of *k in the same words (Table 10.1, pp. 305-306). Lobel's 'West Nuclear' pair (Tawlet-Kalibugan, Salug-Godod) keeps *r and is not a node here (decision lobel-subanen).

name: Proto-East Nuclear Subanen
notes: Southern, Central, Northern and Eastern Subanen, with *r > l (p. 308). Glottolog puts Lapuyan (Southern) Subanun directly under Nuclear Subanen.

name: Western Subanon
notes: Reflexes from Tables 10.4-10.5 (Lobel 2013: 311-312), which list every Proto-Subanen consonant, vowel and vowel sequence; what they show unchanged is unchanged.

name: Duhtu
notes: The Duhtu dialect of Tsou, after Tsuchida (1976) (section 3.9); the representative dialect of Tsou here, so the Tsou entry opens this page. Ross (2012: 1294-1316) takes Tsou to be a first-order branch of PAn, apart from Kanakanavu and Saaroa, which belong to his Nuclear Austronesian; he finds no innovation that defines Tsouic and puts the resemblances down to contact. Sagart (2014: 874-877) defends Tsouic with two sporadic changes and 57 Tsouic-only etyma from Tsuchida (1976). Tsouic is an overlap group here, not a node. The inventory is read directly in Tsuchida’s 1975 dissertation (pp. 85-86): 16 consonants and six vowels, with l [ɾ] and ǰ [d͡ʒ] in loans only; the PAN correspondences stay those of Tsuchida (1976) via Shibata, with conditioned rows from Tsuchida (1975: 305-311) beside them (decision tsuchida-1975).

name: Central Western Plains
notes: Taokas, Babuza (with Favorlang), Papora and Hoanya. Every classification entered puts the four together, so the minimal group that contains them is a node: Li’s Northwestern subgroup (2003: 942-944, with Tsuchida’s 1982: 9-10 innovations), Blust’s Central Western Plains (1999: 45) and Li’s TBPH branch (1985: 260). The larger groups stay overlap groups on the members: Blust’s Western Plains (1996, with Thao) and Li’s North-western and Northern groups (1985). The shared changes (*k > ∅, final *y and *s > ∅, *s > t; Li’s *ŋ > n, which Thao shares) stay on each member, stated from PAN. No proto-language is entered: a group is a node of the tree only, with no rows and no page (decision tree-nodes).

name: Favorlang
notes: Recorded by Dutch missionaries in the 17th century, with more data than Babuza but inconsistent transcriptions; Li (2003: 99 n. 5), following Ogawa (1930a), and Li (2005: 181) take it to be an earlier dialect of Babuza, recorded about 250 years before it. Li (2005: 182-184) gives a PAN > Favorlang table, revised in Ogawa (2003: 6-7). Each row says ‘Label in the source: Favorlang’ (or Favorlang-Babuza, for Ross’s combined column, which is entered on both dialects). Listed under Babuza, as in Glottolog. For the subgroup see Central Western Plains; the larger groupings of Blust (1996) and Li (1985) are overlap groups.

name: Babuza proper
notes: Babuza as recorded in the 20th century (Glottolog’s Poavosa), as against 17th-century Favorlang. One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which Li (2003) leaves out of his main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). Each row says ‘Label in the source: Babuza’ (or Favorlang-Babuza, for Ross’s combined column, also entered on Favorlang). Li (2003: 942-944) puts Taokas and Babuza closest (after Tsuchida 1982: 10). Listed under Babuza, as in Glottolog.

name: Papora-Hoanya
notes: Language node with no rows of its own (Glottolog’s Papora-Hoanya): Papora and Hoanya, which the sources treat as languages, carry the data.

name: Pazeh
region: Western plains of Taiwan; Puli basin
notes: The Auran (Pazeh) dialect of Pazeh-Kaxabu, after Blust (1999b) and Li & Tsuchida (2001) (section 3.6). Blust (1999: 45): Northwest Formosan (Saisiyat, Kulon-Pazeh), by the shifts *C > s and *q > ʔ (the node Northwest Formosan here). Li (1985: 260, 271): with Pazeh, the SP branch of his North-western group, by PAN *g' (Dahl’s *j) > z.

name: Northwest Formosan
notes: Saisiyat and Pazeh-Kaxabu: Blust’s Northwest Formosan (1999: 45, by *C > s and *q > ʔ) and the SP branch of Li’s North-western group (1985: 260, 271, by PAN *g' > z). No classification entered splits the two, so the group is a node; Li’s North-western and Northern groups (1985), which also contain Central Western Plains and Atayalic, stay overlap groups on the members. No proto-language is entered: a group is a node of the tree only, with no rows and no page (decision tree-nodes).

name: Siraya proper

Its two 17th-century varieties, the dialects of the Gospel translations and of the Utrecht Manuscript (Adelaar 2014: 3), are separate lects listed under it, both with this Glottocode, since Glottolog has none for either. Li & Tsuchida’s North group puts Sakizaya with them, against Lin’s tree, and stays an overlap group. No proto-language is entered: a group is a node of the tree only, with no rows and no page (decision tree-nodes).

The coastal dialects distinguish /l/ and /r/; the inland Karkar dialects have merged them as /l/ (p. 216). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

notes: Are-Taupota chain of the Papuan Tip cluster; south coast of the Cape Vogel peninsula, Milne Bay Province. Two dialects, Gapa (east) and Paiwa (west); the sketch, by Catherine McGuckin (Lynch et al. 2002: 297-321), is based on fieldwork in Menapi village in the Gapa area. The Paiwa dialect has /s/ for Gapa /t/ before /u/ (p. 297). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624).

Sketch by Mike Anderson and Malcolm Ross (Lynch et al. 2002: 322-346), based on Anderson & Anderson; describes the dialect of Pamela village on the south coast. The direct reflex of earlier *s is /ð/ (POc *saqat > /ðarə/ 'bad', *sake > /ða/ 'go up'; p. 322). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: 'Ala'ala

Sketch adapted by Malcolm Ross from Symonds (n.d. [1989]) and his own notes on the Oloi dialect (Lynch et al. 2002: 347-361). Glottolog's language is Lala.
