name: Bali (Bali-Vitu)
notes: An isolate within the Meso-Melanesian linkage; French Islands, northwest of Talasea, New Britain. Bali-Vitu has two dialects, Bali (Unea) and Vitu (Garove); the description is of Bali (Ketinerave village). Sketch by Malcolm Ross (Lynch et al. 2002: 362-386). The Bali dialect retains POc final consonants with a following echo vowel (p. 362; Bali /kau'aka/, Vitu /'kaua/ 'dog', p. 363). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 623).

name: Kaulong
notes: Pasismanua chain of the Southwest New Britain linkage. Data collected at Au village in the northern part of the western dialect area. Sketch adapted by Malcolm Ross from manuscripts by Craig Throop and his own fieldnotes (Lynch et al. 2002: 387-409).

name: Siar
notes: South New Ireland/Northwest Solomonic linkage of the Meso-Melanesian cluster; southern tip of New Ireland and Lambom Island. Sketch by Malcolm Ross (Lynch et al. 2002: 410-425), largely from his fieldnotes (Lambom Island and Bakok village). Intervocalic /ɸ/ and /w/ have merged at Bakok, and at Lambom [β] has largely been replaced by [w] in the last 20 years (p. 411). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: Taiof
notes: North Bougainville linkage; Taiof Island, west of the northern tip of Bougainville. Wurm and Hattori's atlas treats it as part of the Saposa language (Glottolog has it as a dialect of Saposa, sapo1253), but the sketch, by Malcolm Ross (Lynch et al. 2002: 426-439), describes it separately. The phonemes /c/ and /ñ/ arose from allophones of earlier /t/ and /n/ before /i/ (p. 426).

name: Banoni
notes: Southwest Bougainville. The sketch, adapted by John Lynch and Malcolm Ross (Lynch et al. 2002: 440-455), describes the inland dialect of Mabesi (Lincoln) and Mariga (Ross's fieldnotes). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 623).

name: Sisiqa
notes: Central Choiseul, Solomon Islands (Northwest Solomonic). Tryon and Hackman classify it as a dialect of East Choiseul, but it is different enough from its western neighbour Babatana to be treated separately. Sketch by Malcolm Ross from his fieldnotes, Ghaghara village (Lynch et al. 2002: 456-466).

name: Roviana
notes: Northwest Solomonic; Roviana lagoon, New Georgia, Solomon Islands. Sketch by Simon Corston-Oliver from his own fieldwork (Lynch et al. 2002: 467-497). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Kokota
notes: Santa Isabel, Solomon Islands (Goveo, Sisiga, Hurepelo). Sketch by Bill Palmer from his field research in Goveo village (Lynch et al. 2002: 498-524). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 625).

name: Gela
notes: Guadalcanal grouping of Southeast Solomonic (after Tryon and Hackman); central Solomon Islands. Three dialects; the sketch, by Terry Crowley from information from John Kouni (Lynch et al. 2002: 525-537), describes Small Nggela. Big Nggela /h/ corresponds systematically to /z/ in the other dialects, and in it the voiced stops are prenasalised in all environments (Fox; pp. 525-526). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624).

name: Longgu
notes: Southeast Solomonic (Longgu/Malaita/Makira); northeastern coast of Guadalcanal. Sketch by Deborah Hill from her fieldwork in Bambasu and Nangali (Lynch et al. 2002: 538-561). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 625).

name: Arosi
notes: Southeast Solomonic (Makira); western Makira (San Cristobal), Solomon Islands. Three dialects; the sketch, adapted by John Lynch and Rex Horoi (Lynch et al. 2002: 562-572), is based largely on the Wango (western) dialect, the basis of Fox's dictionary. Vowel length is phonemic (long vowels entered, decision lrc2002-readings). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 623).

name: Sakao
notes: North Central Vanuatu; Port Olry and Hog Harbour area, eastern Espiritu Santo. Sketch adapted by Terry Crowley from Guy, the only published description (Lynch et al. 2002: 599-607). The Glottocode is the one in Ross et al. (2023); Glottolog has it as a dialect. Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Tamambo
notes: Northern Vanuatu linkage; Malo island, south of Espiritu Santo. Sketch by Dorothy Jauncey from her fieldwork (Lynch et al. 2002: 608-625), where the name is spelled Tamabo [tamaᵐbo]. It describes the western dialect; the eastern dialect, Tamapo, lacks prenasalised voiced stops and differs in other details of phonology and morphology (p. 608). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: Raga
notes: North Central Vanuatu; northern third of Pentecost. Sketch abstracted by Terry Crowley from Walsh, with material from Walsh & Liñi and George Hinge (Lynch et al. 2002: 626-637). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Vinmavis
notes: Malakula (North Central Vanuatu); the village of Vinmavis on the west coast of northern Malakula; local name Nefe'ei. Sketch by Terry Crowley from data provided by Joemela Simeon of Vinmavis (Lynch et al. 2002: 638-649). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626).

name: Port Sandwich
notes: Southwestern Malakula, Vanuatu (nine villages around Lamap); no indigenous name. Sketch adapted by Terry Crowley from Charpentier (Lynch et al. 2002: 650-659). The phonetic sequences [mb], [mbw], [ndr], [ŋɡ] are attested; their phonemic status is problematic (p. 651). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Southeast Ambrym
notes: North Central Vanuatu; southeastern Ambrym (eighteen villages) and a relocated community at Mele-Maat, Efate; most closely related to Paama. Sketch adapted by Terry Crowley from Parker and material from Wilfred Tasso (Lynch et al. 2002: 660-670). Vowel length is contrastive but has a very low functional load (long vowels entered, decision lrc2002-readings). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: Lamen
notes: Epi subgroup of North and Central Vanuatu; Lamen island off northwest Epi; closest relatives Lewo and Bierebo. Sketch by Robert Early (Lynch et al. 2002: 671-680). Vowel length is phonemic (long vowels entered, decision lrc2002-readings).

name: Mele (Ifira-Mele)
notes: Samoic-Outlier Polynesian; Mele village, northwest of Port Vila, Efate. Ifira-Mele has two dialects, Ifira and Mele; the sketch, by Ross Clark (Lynch et al. 2002: 681-693), is based exclusively on the Mele dialect (fieldwork 1974-1986, principal authority Edwin Nganga). Vowel length is phonemic for all vowels and consonants occur geminate (long vowels entered, decision lrc2002-readings).

name: Sye
notes: Southern Vanuatu subgroup (Southern Oceanic linkage); Erromango. Sketch by Terry Crowley, an abridged version of Crowley, based on information supplied largely by Edward Nalial (Lynch et al. 2002: 694-722). An underlying sixth vowel /ə/, realised only as zero or [o], has to be set up for the alternations of suffixed morphemes (p. 695). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: Anejom̃
notes: Southern Vanuatu subgroup (Southern Oceanic linkage); Aneityum. Sketch by John Lynch from fieldwork in Port Vila and on Aneityum (Lynch et al. 2002: 723-752). Vowel length is contrastive (not entered). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 623).

name: Cèmuhî
notes: North New Caledonian subgroup; northeast New Caledonia. Sketch abstracted by John Lynch from Rivierre, with Rivierre. Cèmuhî distinguishes three register tones, high, mid and low, plus a 'neutral' tone that harmonises with the preceding syllable (p. 753); tones are not entered as phonemes. After a nasal /e/-/ɛ/ and /o/-/ɔ/ are neutralised; after labio-velars only /i e ɔ a/ occur (p. 754). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624).

name: Xârâcùù
notes: South New Caledonian subgroup; Canala area, southern New Caledonia. Sketch abstracted by John Lynch from Moyse-Faurie (Lynch et al. 2002: 765-775). The oral/nasal contrast appears to be neutralised (as a nasal vowel) before a nasal or prenasalised stop, but only intra-morphemically (p. 765). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 629).

name: Iaai
notes: Loyalties subgroup of New Caledonian (with Nengone and Drehu); central Ouvéa. Sketch abstracted by John Lynch, based mainly on Ozanne-Rivierre, with data from Tryon and Ozanne-Rivierre. The contrast between velarised and simple bilabials is neutralised (as a simple bilabial) before rounded vowels and /a/; /ɛ/ and /a/ are neutralised as [ɛ] after /ü ɸ β/ (pp. 776-777). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624). Under Proto-Loyalties (Lynch 2003b; decision lynch2003b-ploy).

name: Rotuman
notes: An isolate within the Central Pacific linkage, closest to the Fijian languages; its lexicon has many Polynesian loanwords (Biggs 1965). Sketch adapted by Hans Schmidt, based largely on Churchward with material from Hocart, Milner, Besnier, Blevins, Geraghty and his own fieldwork (Lynch et al. 2002: 815-832). Rotuman originally had the five POc vowels /i u e o a/; five more developed through metathesis and related processes: /ü/ < u + i, /ø/ < o + i, /œ/ < o + e, /æ/ < a + i and a + e, /ɔ/ < a + u (p. 816). Vowel length is not phonemic (Blevins, contra Churchward). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Nadrogā
notes: Western Fijian (Central Pacific linkage); southwestern Viti Levu. Sketch by Paul Geraghty (Lynch et al. 2002: 833-847). Glottolog has Nadrogā as a dialect of Western Viti Levu-Yasawas Fijian. Length is phonemically contrastive with all five vowels (p. 835; not entered). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626).

name: Western Fijian
notes: Language node for its dialect Nadrogā, described in Nadrogā (Lynch et al. 2002: 833-847).

name: Niuafo'ou
notes: Samoic Outlier subgroup of Nuclear Polynesian, with its closest relative East 'Uvean; overlaid with extensive borrowing from Tongan. Northernmost island of Tonga. Sketch abstracted by Robert Early from Tsukamoto (Lynch et al. 2002: 848-864). Phonetically long vowels are analysed as geminate sequences (p. 848).

name: Proto-South Halmahera–West New Guinea
notes: Thirty-eight languages of southern Halmahera, Raja Ampat, Cenderawasih Bay and the Mamberamo mouth; sister of Oceanic within Eastern Malayo-Polynesian; time depth up to 3,500 years, homeland most likely southern Cenderawasih Bay (Kamholz 2024: 181). Kamholz gives the defining changes from PMP, since little has been reconstructed at the PCEMP and PEMP levels (p. 181 n. 1); his change 12, lexically specific syncope of the penultimate vowel (C₁VC₂V > C₁C₂V), is not a segment correspondence and is not entered (p. 182). The Glottolog family of the same name (sout3229) has the same membership.

name: Proto-Yaur-Yerisiam
notes: Defined by a single innovation, PMP *ŋ > ∅; Kamholz considers the subgroup tentative (2024: 184). In his tree (Table 14.1) it sits under Proto-Southwest Cenderawasih Bay (itself tentative, defined by PMP *z > ∅ and an irregular change in *punti) and Proto-Nuclear Cenderawasih Bay (defined by morphological innovations); both are entered as nodes without changes of their own (decision shwng-nodes).

name: Proto-Raja Ampat–South Halmahera
notes: Defined by PMP *R > ∅ and the 1sg/2sg subject infix *‹y› (Kamholz 2024: 184), after a proposal by Remijsen. Its subgroups Proto-South Halmahera and Proto-Central-Eastern South Halmahera are defined by morphological innovations only and are not entered (decision shwng-nodes).

name: Pom
notes: Central Yapen, Cenderawasih Bay; its inventory is typical of the Yapen languages (Gasser et al. 2024: 631). Kamholz (2024: 183) classifies it as Proto-Nuclear Cenderawasih Bay > Proto-Yapen > Proto-Western Yapen > Proto-Central Yapen, all defined by morphological innovations; entered so (decision shwng-nodes, reverted by the user).

name: Yaur
notes: Southwest Cenderawasih Bay. Yaur has contrastive vowel length and two tones, High and Low, associated with morae (Gasser et al. 2024: 631, 633); not entered as phonemes. Yaur does not permit final consonants (p. 633).

name: Patani
notes: Central-Eastern South Halmahera (Kamholz 2024: 183). Patani allows triconsonantal clusters, and an epenthetic vowel copying the vowel of the preceding syllable is inserted before an initial cluster when the preceding word ends in a consonant (Gasser et al. 2024: 632-633).

name: Proto-Chamic
notes: Developments from PMP after Thurgood (1999), as listed by Adelaar (2005: 373-374); ten of them are shared with Malayic. Not entered as rows: cluster reduction; nasals becoming homorganic to a following stop (a following voiced stop being lost); occasional homorganic nasal accretion between initial schwa and a following stop; occasional *j > ḷ (as printed); occasional reduction of the penultimate vowel (items 9, 10, 12, 15-16).

name: Proto-Balinese-Sasak-Sumbawa
notes: Developments from PMP after Mbete (1990), as listed by Adelaar (2005: 374); eight are shared with Malayic. Adelaar reconstructs the reflexes of PMP *-ay and *-aw as PBSS *-ey and *-ow, where Mbete has *-[i,e] and *-o, *-[i,o] (p. 359). Mbete distinguishes a Balinese branch and a Sasak-Sumbawa branch (p. 358); Proto-Sasak-Sumbawa is not entered. Not entered as a row: frequent homorganic nasal accretion between initial schwa and a following stop (item 12).

name: Balinese
notes: Developments from PBSS after Mbete (1990), in Adelaar (2005: 374), with the reflexes of *r from his section 2 (p. 364). Old Balinese keeps *r and *h. Not entered as a row: *ə assimilated to the following vowel after the loss of *-r- (item 18).

name: Sasak
notes: Developments from PBSS after Mbete (1990), in Adelaar (2005: 375); Sasak and Sumbawa form the other primary branch of BSS.

name: Sumbawa
notes: Developments from PBSS after Mbete (1990), in Adelaar (2005: 375). Not entered as a row: contraction of adjacent vowels, which did not take place in the Sumbawa Besar dialect (item 22).

name: Javanese
notes: Developments from PMP after Nothofer (1975), in Adelaar (2005: 375-376); seven are shared with Malayic. Adelaar excludes Javanese from Malayo-Sumbawan. ò is written ɔ here. Not entered as rows: in modern Javanese, nasals become homorganic to following consonants, and non-nasal clusters are reduced to their second consonant (items 13-14).

name: Sundanese
notes: Developments from PMP after Nothofer (1975), in Adelaar (2005: 376); 'fewer than six' are shared with Malayic. /ə/ also exists but is a loan phoneme. Adelaar puts Sundanese in Malayo-Sumbawan as a branch of its own.

name: Madurese
notes: Developments from PMP after Nothofer (1975), in Adelaar (2005: 376); four are shared with Malayic. è and ò are written ɛ and ɔ here. Not entered as rows: the fortition of non-final *w and *y (no outcome stated); the dental series d, dʰ, t contrasting with a retroflex series, with no conditioning factor (item 14, considered due to contact); gemination after schwa (item 15). Adelaar puts Madurese in Malayo-Sumbawan as a branch of its own.

name: Proto-Central Pacific
notes: Ancestor of Fijian, Rotuman and Polynesian, a subgroup first proposed and named by George Grace. Geraghty (1986: 289) reconstructs its sound system without assuming any internal subgrouping, while holding that 'a compelling case for Central Pacific has yet to be made' (1983: 352-366). His PCP is based on the Proto-Eastern Oceanic of Geraghty (1983), with *x added. A five-vowel system with phonemic length (p. 309, n. 5); length is not entered. Proto-Polynesian stays under POc (decision ppn-parent) and is listed as a proposed daughter; Geraghty's PCP > PPn rows wait for decision geraghty1986-ppn. Glottocode cent2060 (Central Pacific linkage), same membership.

name: Proto-Fijian
notes: Geraghty's own reconstruction (1986: 289). Geraghty and Pawley have suggested that some features found in both Eastern and Western Fijian may have diffused after the break-up of Proto-Fijian (Geraghty 1986: 309, n. 3). Glottolog has no Fijian clade (it splits Central Pacific into Western Fijian and Tokalau Fijian, the latter with Polynesian), so no Glottocode (decision geraghty1986-pfj). Vowels are not discussed and are taken as unchanged (inherit assumed-unchanged). A proposed, not established node (decision geraghty1986-pfj): Western Fijian (Nadrogā) stays under POc and lists it as a proposed parent.

name: Proto-Southern Vanuatu
notes: Reconstructed by Lynch (2001) from Proto Erromango, Proto Tanna and Anejom, with its development from POc. Lynch (2001: 13, 184) groups the Southern Vanuatu languages as Erromango (Sye, Ura, Utaha), Tanna (Northern: North Tanna, Whitesands, Lenakel; Southern: Southwest Tanna, Kwamera) and Anejom. Lynch places Southern Vanuatu in Southern Oceanic (pp. 6, 190) but enters no PSOc changes of his own; the Southern Oceanic group (soc) is a linkage here (decision pocr-parents). Changes in canonical form that are not segment correspondences are in the notes only: loss of pretonic vowels (*na lima-ña > Lenakel nelman), accretion of an initial vowel to most verbs and of the article *na to most nouns, and retention of POc final consonants, which the Erromangan languages tend to lose after nasals and Anejom loses except *r (p. 14; Table 4.1, p. 102). Glottocode sout2868 (Southern Vanuatu), same membership.

name: Proto-Erromango
notes: Lynch (2001: 13-91). Utaha (Ifo) data are 'highly tentative, based as they are on the most fragmentary of data' and are given only in the tables of correspondences (p. 13). Lynch also reconstructs medial clusters *n + *r (Sye nr, Ura d-, -d-, -n; p. 42) and *n + *t (Sye nt, Ura d; pp. 53, 55), from the accreted article and from compounds; these are not entered as phonemes. Glottocode erro1239 (Erromanga), same membership.

name: Proto-Tanna
notes: Lynch (2001: 13-99). Two subgroups, Northern and Southern Tanna (p. 13; justified in ch. 8). POc *l, *r and *R merged as PTn *r (p. 45). Glottocode tann1242 (Tanna), same membership.

name: Proto-Northern Tanna
notes: Given by Lynch (2001) only in Appendix I (pp. 201-203) and in the discussion of the liquids and sibilants (pp. 45-47, 66): PTn *r split into PNT *l and *i, and PTn *h into *h and *z. Glottocode nort3218 (Northern Tanna linkage in Glottolog), same membership.

name: Proto-Southern Tanna
notes: Given by Lynch (2001) only in Appendix I (pp. 201-203), where every PST phoneme is the same as in PTn (*q is marked '?'). Glottocode sout3195 (Southern Tanna), same membership.

name: Ura
notes: Erromango; moribund (Lynch 2001: 4-5). Lynch (2001: 7) quotes Terry Crowley on the considerable variation between [l] and [r] in Ura transcriptions. Many Ura words with medial t are probably Sye loans (Lynch 2001: 55). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 629).

name: Utaha
notes: Extinct language of Erromango. Lynch's Utaha reflexes are 'highly tentative, based as they are on the most fragmentary of data' (2001: 13), and the vowels could not be worked out (p. 91). Glottolog name Ifo.

name: North Tanna
notes: The dialect Lynch cites has, besides the voiceless stops, an incomplete set of prenasalised voiced stops /ᵐbʷ ᵐb ⁿd/; other dialects have the Lenakel system (2001: 7). It is not clear whether North Tanna and Whitesands have /w/ (p. 7, n. 6); not entered. Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Whitesands
notes: Same consonant system as Lenakel, perhaps also with /fʷ/ (Lynch 2001: 7); whether it has /w/ is not clear (p. 7, n. 6), and /w/ is not entered. Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 629).

name: Lenakel
notes: Lynch's own field language (2001: 7). Vowel length is contrastive, mostly in final syllables (p. 8); not entered. Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 625).

name: Southwest Tanna
notes: Same system as Kwamera, except that most dialects have /l/ for /r/ (Lynch 2001: 7-8); the Mess dialect has r (p. 45, n. 15). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628).

name: Kwamera
notes: Kwamera fluctuates between s and h more than the other Tanna languages (Lynch 2001: 65). Vowel length is contrastive (p. 8); not entered. Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 625).

name: Zuanga-Yuanga
notes: Language node for its dialects Gomen Yuanga and Bondé Yuanga (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 192-193).

name: Gomen Yuanga
notes: Northern New Caledonian. Keeps dental /t̪/ (< POc *s) apart from retroflex /ʈ/ (< POc *d, Ross's *r), while POc *t became k (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 192-193). Glottocode thua1237 (Zuanga) is an identification (decision nc1992-lects).

name: Bondé Yuanga
notes: Northern New Caledonian; data from Corne's manuscript dictionary (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 206). Glottocode juan1250 (Yuanga dialect) is an identification (decision nc1992-lects).

name: Nêlêmwa-Nixumwak
notes: Language node for its dialect Kumak (Nixumwak).

name: Kumak
notes: Northern New Caledonian (Koumac); data from Haudricourt (via Ozanne-Rivierre 1992).

name: Nyelâyu
notes: Far North New Caledonian. Some spontaneous nasalisation of a in the Belep variety may attest an earlier initial glottal (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 194). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627), which has Nyelâyu as bala1316.

name: Pwapwâ
notes: Northern New Caledonian (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992).

name: Pwaamei
notes: Northern New Caledonian (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Nemi
notes: Northern New Caledonian, Hienghène region (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626), which prints the Glottocode as nemi124.

name: Haveke
notes: Northern New Caledonian (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992).

name: Numèè
notes: Extreme southern New Caledonian; keeps POc *q apart from *k, as Drubea does (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 195). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 627).

name: Drubea
notes: Extreme southern New Caledonian. Vowel nasality is phonological only after oral consonants (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 199, after Rivierre's study of the Far South dialects). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624).

name: Drehu
notes: Loyalty Islands (Lifou). Its voiced /b/ comes from English loans; prenasalised consonants no longer exist in the Loyalties (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 197). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 624). Under Proto-Loyalties (Lynch 2003b; decision lynch2003b-ploy).

name: Nengone
notes: Loyalty Islands (Maré) (Ozanne-Rivierre 1992: 197). Coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 626). Under Proto-Loyalties (Lynch 2003b; decision lynch2003b-ploy).

name: Proto-Barito
notes: The nine Barito lects of Smith (2017a: 168-182, Tables 56-57). Smith finds no phonological innovation of quality for Proto-Barito and calls Barito a linkage (pp. 170-171, §2.7.4-2.7.5); the node is entered by the user's revert of decision smith-barito (23 Nov 2026), with what Smith notes there: *R is kept and final *-a becomes *-ə. Hudson's West and East Barito stay overlap groups. Yakan, entered from the same tables as a representative of Sama-Bajaw, is not Barito. No glottocode: Glottolog's Barito groups are not checked against these nine lects.

name: Proto-Nuclear Puyuma
notes: Yeh (2024: 193-194, fig. 6.1): Nanwang (with Apapulu) against Proto-Nuclear Puyuma, which splits into Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek (Alripay, Pinaski; Mulivelivek, Danadanaw), Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw and Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan. Spirantization of the voiced stops (*b > β, *d̪ > ð, *ɖ > ʐ, *ɡ > h) is the change of this node; Nanwang alone keeps the voiced stops. Ting (1978), as cited by Teng (2008: 5), has the same grouping of the non-Nanwang dialects (decision puyuma-ting). No Glottolog languoid.

name: Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek
notes: Yeh (2024: 193-194, fig. 6.1): Nanwang (with Apapulu) against Proto-Nuclear Puyuma, which splits into Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek (Alripay, Pinaski; Mulivelivek, Danadanaw), Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw and Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan. Entered as a node below Proto-Nuclear Puyuma (decision yeh-puyuma-tree). No changes of its own are entered: the rows of Yeh's Tables 4.29-4.31 are stated for each dialect and stay on the dialects. Its own innovations, if Yeh states any (pp. 193-194), were not re-read for this entry. No Glottolog languoid.

name: Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw
notes: Yeh (2024: 193-194, fig. 6.1): Nanwang (with Apapulu) against Proto-Nuclear Puyuma, which splits into Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek (Alripay, Pinaski; Mulivelivek, Danadanaw), Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw and Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan. Entered as a node below Proto-Nuclear Puyuma (decision yeh-puyuma-tree). No changes of its own are entered: the rows of Yeh's Tables 4.29-4.31 are stated for each dialect and stay on the dialects. Its own innovations, if Yeh states any (pp. 193-194), were not re-read for this entry. No Glottolog languoid.

name: Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan
notes: Yeh (2024: 193-194, fig. 6.1): Nanwang (with Apapulu) against Proto-Nuclear Puyuma, which splits into Proto-Alripay-Mulivelivek (Alripay, Pinaski; Mulivelivek, Danadanaw), Proto-Likavung-Tamalrakaw and Proto-Katripulr-Kasavakan. Entered as a node below Proto-Nuclear Puyuma (decision yeh-puyuma-tree). No changes of its own are entered: the rows of Yeh's Tables 4.29-4.31 are stated for each dialect and stay on the dialects. Its own innovations, if Yeh states any (pp. 193-194), were not re-read for this entry. No Glottolog languoid.

name: Proto-Wetar-Galolen
notes: Overlapping subgroup in the classification tree of Grimes & Edwards (2026: 251) (§4.8.2): Wetar and Galolen, sharing *z > s; *b > **f; *-ay > e; *-aw > o. It overlaps with Nuclear Wetar-Atauro (Wetar and Atauro); by the user's choice (decision ge-overlap, 23 Nov 2026) Wetar-Galolen is Wetar's parent in the tree and Proto-Nuclear Wetar-Atauro is its proposed parent. Glottolog 5.4 has a Wetar-Galolen (weta1247); its membership was not checked in this session, so the glottocode is left blank (decision ge-overlap).

name: Proto-Nuclear Wetar-Atauro
notes: Overlapping subgroup in the classification tree of Grimes & Edwards (2026: 251) (§4.8.2): Atauro and Wetar, sharing *j > +fr, r; *R/*d > r. It overlaps with Wetar-Galolen, which is Wetar's parent in the tree (decision ge-overlap); Wetar is a proposed daughter here and carries these changes itself (composed). No Glottolog languoid of this name; no glottocode.

name: Proto-Greater Dusunic
notes: Lobel (2013: ch. 11, §11.1.2): Greater Dusunic = Dusunic, Bisaya-Lotud and Paitanic, which share innovations 2-8 (pp. 365-367). Entered as a node by the user's revert of decision lobel-swsabah (23 Nov 2026), although the standing rule for Lobel holds back intermediate nodes above established groups. Its rows are the changes all its members share, taken up from them. Glottocode grea1293 (Glottolog's Greater Dusunic, as given in decision lobel-swsabah; its membership was not re-checked).

name: Proto-Greater Murutic
notes: Lobel (2013: ch. 11, §11.1.2): Greater Murutic = core Murutic, Papar and Tatana (pp. 367, §11.4.1). Entered as a node by the user's revert of decision lobel-swsabah (23 Nov 2026), although the standing rule for Lobel holds back intermediate nodes above established groups. Its rows are the changes all its members share, taken up from them. Glottocode grea1294 (Glottolog's Greater Murutic, as given in decision lobel-swsabah; its membership was not re-checked).

name: Pije
orthography_note: Practical orthography of Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre (1982: 17): h before a consonant marks aspiration (ph, hm, hl), b d j g bw are prenasalised, ny ng = ɲ ŋ, a circumflex marks a nasal vowel, doubled vowels are long. IPA here.
notes: Northern New Caledonian, Hienghène region: Tiendanite, Ouenghip, Tiouandé (Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982: 9-10). With Fwâi and Nemi it keeps old POc dentals before *a as apicals, which Jawe palatalises (§1.2); it has a thematic vowel a in possessed nouns where the others have e (§1.3); the old post-nasalised consonants appear as aspirates followed by nasal vowels (§1.4). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).

name: Fwâi
orthography_note: As for Pije (Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982: 17-18). IPA here.
notes: Northern New Caledonian: lower Hienghène valley, Tanghène valley and the coast from Pindache to the mouth of the Ouaième; it is replacing Nemi in the villages north of that mouth (Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982: 18). Oral stops and strong continuants occur only in loans (p. 18). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).

name: Jawe
orthography_note: As for Pije; ch is written c before a nasal vowel; ü and ë are [y] and [œ] (Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982: 21-23). IPA here.
notes: Northern New Caledonian: east coast from Colnett to Tchambouène, the Ouaième valley at Pangou, and the central chain at Ouayaguette (Wevia) and Ouahat. Two varieties: Yambé (Y), whose system is entered here, and Wevia (W), which keeps the post-nasalised consonants of Nemi 2, at least initially; in Yambé they became aspirated stops followed by nasal vowels (Haudricourt & Ozanne-Rivierre 1982: 21). Jawe palatalises old dentals before *a (§1.2). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).

name: Yapese
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of Jensen (1977a: 13-38): ch = ʈ, q = ʔ, th = θ, s = ʂ, b d g j = β ð ɣ ʐ, ng = ŋ, y = j; an apostrophe marks a glottalized consonant (ejective pʼ tʼ kʼ fʼ θʼ; mˀ nˀ ŋˀ lˀ wˀ jˀ); vowels i e ë ö o ä a u = i e ɛ ɵ ɔ æ ɑ u, long ii ee ea oe oo ae aa uu (decisions jensen1977-symbols, jensen1977-vowels). Ross's (1996) comparative transcription is respelled (c > ʈ, v > β, fˀ > fʼ); his vˀ is kept.
notes: Western Micronesia; not Nuclear Micronesian. Ross (1996) separates five strata of Austronesian vocabulary: Sets A and B from non-Oceanic sources (an older stage of Palauan or a lect close to it; an unidentified conservative language), Set C from an Oceanic source outside Nuclear Micronesian, Set D and its variant Set UW from Nuclear Micronesian (mostly Western Trukic) and recent Ulithian and Woleaian loans, and a small Set E from a Central Pacific source (pp. 128-131). Set C is the inherited stratum: the bound morphemes reflect it, so Yapese is Oceanic (p. 130). Ross tentatively links its inherited stratum with the Admiralties, as an early offshoot (§2.3, pp. 143-151); there is no Admiralties node here. Every Yapese word must begin and end with a consonant, so a glottal stop is added to vowel-initial and vowel-final words (p. 131). Glottocode and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023). Ross's superscript o (mᵒ) marks a rounding effect on the neighbouring vowels, not on the consonant; the exact values of c and of the glottalised consonants wait for a source (decision ross1996-symbols).

name: Tomoip
region: Pomio and Talasea districts, New Britain, Papua New Guinea
orthography_note: Barlow & Ross write IPA (β, ʝ, ŋ).
notes: Oceanic language of New Britain, once thought non-Austronesian; about 23 percent of a 1,050-item wordlist is identified as Oceanic (Barlow & Ross 2025: 323). Barlow & Ross place it with the New Ireland languages under a proposed Proto-Tomoip-New Ireland, sharing the split of POc *p into *p and *v and the merger of *k and *q followed by a split into *k and *ɣ (pp. 355-358); Ross (1988: 258) had derived Tomoip from New Ireland. Neither node is entered (decision barlowross2025-tree), so the parent is POc. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).

name: Nêlêmwa
region: Poum and the far northern islets, New Caledonia
notes: Variety of Nêlêmwa-Nixumwak (nel), from Bril's fieldwork (Bril 2020: 197-198). It differs from Nixumwak by spirantising the aspirated voiceless consonants: nix kʰ, pʰw, pʰ, tʰ, cʰ = nel x/ɣ, fw, f [ɸ], [β], tʰ/rʰ, ʃ (p. 198). Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4 (Nêlêmwa, a dialect of Nêlêmwa-Nixumwak); coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023), which print the Glottocode with a character missing (nene125).

name: Austral
notes: Language node for the Austral dialects Rurutu, Ra'ivavae, Rimatara and the extinct Tupua'i (Tubuai) (Charpentier & François 2015: 76, Table 5). Glottocode and ISO code from Glottolog 5.4.

name: Ra'ivavae
orthography_note: Atlas transcription: the glottal stop is written with a reversed apostrophe, ‘ (p. 93); vowel length with a macron.
notes: Dialect of Austral; survey point 18 of the atlas. Its reflex of PPn *l, *r is a stop [ɡ] (Charpentier & François 2015: 93). Eight consonants (Table 6). Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4; coordinates of the island.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the consonants Table 6 gives as identical with the Proto-Tahitic ones.

name: Maupiti
orthography_note: Atlas transcription: the glottal stop is written with a reversed apostrophe, ‘ (p. 93); vowel length with a macron.
notes: Variety of Maupiti, 'sometimes described as strange', survey point 6 (Charpentier & François 2015: 79, 93): k (and t) for Tahitian t, ten consonants. Not in Glottolog 5.4 (a Leeward Islands variety of Tahitian); coordinates of the island.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the consonants Table 6 gives as identical with the Proto-Tahitic ones.

name: Nuku Hiva
orthography_note: Atlas transcription: the glottal stop is written with a reversed apostrophe, ‘ (p. 93); vowel length with a macron.
notes: North Marquesan variety, survey point 1 of the atlas (Charpentier & François 2015: 77, 93). Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4 (a dialect of North Marquesan); coordinates of the island.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the consonants Table 6 gives as identical with the Proto-East Polynesian Distal ones.

name: Ua Huna
orthography_note: Atlas transcription: the glottal stop is written with a reversed apostrophe, ‘ (p. 93); vowel length with a macron.
notes: North Marquesan variety, survey point 2 of the atlas (Charpentier & François 2015: 77, 93). The atlas names the survey point Ua Huna (Map 3, Table 6); Map 3 also has 'Nuku Hiva (Ua Huka)', so Ua Huna is not taken to be the island Ua Huka (Glottolog uahu1237); no Glottocode.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the consonants Table 6 gives as identical with the Proto-East Polynesian Distal ones.

name: Ua Pou
orthography_note: Atlas transcription: the glottal stop is written with a reversed apostrophe, ‘ (p. 93); vowel length with a macron.
notes: North Marquesan variety, survey point 3 of the atlas (Charpentier & François 2015: 77, 93). Glottocode from Glottolog 5.4 (a dialect of North Marquesan); coordinates of the island.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the consonants Table 6 gives as identical with the Proto-East Polynesian Distal ones.

name: Proto-Vanikoro
notes: Teanu, Lovono and Tanema. François (2009: 5-6) argues for it from the paragogic vowel, *t > k before u and lexical innovations (Table 2), against Ross & Næss (2007: 473), for whom 'no innovations define Vanikoro'; Lackey & Boerger (2021: 383-388) give a set of ordered shared changes ((103), Table 3). In the main tree, as the parent of the three languages (decision temotu-tree, reverted by the user); no Glottolog clade (Glottolog has Utupua-Vanikoro only).

name: Proto-Temotu
notes: Ancestor of the Oceanic (non-Polynesian) languages of Temotu Province, Solomon Islands: Reefs-Santa Cruz, Utupua and Vanikoro. A primary subgroup of Oceanic, not part of any other known subgroup (Ross & Næss 2007: 471), defined by the merger of POc *r and *l as *l (pp. 471-472) and of *s, *c and *j as *s (Lackey & Boerger 2021: 388-389), and by the loss of the initial consonant in three etyma (*Rumwaq, *lima, *ñamuk; Ross & Næss 2007: 472). Conservative: it kept POc final consonants (Ross & Næss 2007: 464), POc prosody, *k apart from *q and perhaps *ñ apart from *n (Lackey & Boerger 2021: 370, 393); *q was perhaps lenited to a fricative (x or χ) that later languages restored or lost (p. 390). Whether a Proto-Temotu node is needed at all has been doubted (François, p.c. in Lackey & Boerger 2021: 370). Glottocode temo1244 (Temotu).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Proto-Temotu was conservative, 'possibly trivially close to POC in structure' (Lackey & Boerger 2021: 370).

name: Proto-Reefs-Santa Cruz
notes: Äiwoo (Reef Islands) and the Santa Cruz languages Natügu, Nalögo, Noipä and Engdewu (Nagu). Defined by truncation of the final syllable of nouns and by syncope (Ross & Næss 2007: 465-467), which Lackey & Boerger (2021: 376-382) derive from POc stress, and by loss of initial *t- in *taŋis (Ross & Næss 2007: 473). Lackey & Boerger (2021: 370) also have a Santa Cruz node (Engdewu, Nalögo, Noipä, Natügu), not entered. Tree after decision temotu-tree: subgroups that both Ross & Næss (2007) and Lackey & Boerger (2021) accept are in the main tree.

name: Proto-Utupua
notes: Nebao (Amba), Asuboa (Asumboa) and Tanibili (Tanimbili). Defined by the loss of POc word-final *-r, *-s, *-q and *-R and the complete loss of *R (Ross & Næss 2007: 473), and the loss of *s (with *c, *j) between vowels (Lackey & Boerger 2021: 388). Ross & Næss put it under Utupua-Vanikoro; Lackey & Boerger directly under Proto-Temotu. Tree after decision temotu-tree: subgroups that both Ross & Næss (2007) and Lackey & Boerger (2021) accept are in the main tree.

name: Proto-Utupua-Vanikoro
notes: Ross & Næss's (2007: 473) subgroup of the Utupua and Vanikoro languages, with four branches (Utupua, Buma, Vano, Tanema), defined by the loss of nonfinal POc *q (weak evidence, as Santa Cruz shares it) and by the diphthongization of final schwa, which cuts across the two islands (pp. 468-469). Lackey & Boerger (2021: 389-392) reject it; it has no daughters in the main tree (decision temotu-tree).

name: Äiwoo
region: Reef Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
orthography_note: Ross & Næss write the prenasalised stops b, d, g and the RSC vowels as in the practical orthographies; reflexes here are in IPA, with source_form where they differ.
notes: Data from Næss's fieldwork (Ross & Næss 2007: 459). Practical orthography: ny = /ɲ/, ng = /ŋ/; /n/~/ɲ/, /t/~/s/ and /d/~/j/ are neutralised before /i/ (p. 461). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 2 gives the other consonants as the parent's; the vowels, which Ross & Næss call complex (p. 463), are not described and are taken as unchanged.

region: Santa Cruz (Nendö), Temotu Province, Solomon Islands

inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 2 gives the other consonants as the parent's; the vowels, which Ross & Næss call complex (p. 463), are not described and are taken as unchanged.

region: Santa Cruz (Nendö), Temotu Province, Solomon Islands
orthography_note: Ross & Næss write the prenasalised stops b, d, g and the RSC vowels as in the practical orthographies; reflexes here are in IPA, with source_form where they differ.
notes: Engdewu was formerly called Nagu or Nanggu (Lackey & Boerger 2021: 369). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023) (no coordinates there).

orthography_note: Ross & Næss write the prenasalised stops b, d, g and the RSC vowels as in the practical orthographies; reflexes here are in IPA, with source_form where they differ.
notes: Data from Tryon & Hackman (1983) (Ross & Næss 2007: 459; Lackey & Boerger 2021: 368). Nebao nh is the regular reflex of *pVn- (Ross & Næss 2007: 469). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).

name: Asumboa
orthography_note: Ross & Næss write the prenasalised stops b, d, g and the RSC vowels as in the practical orthographies; reflexes here are in IPA, with source_form where they differ.
notes: Data from Tryon & Hackman (1983). Ross & Næss (2007: 471) write Asumboa; Table 2 has Asu. Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 2 gives the other consonants as the parent's; the vowels, which Ross & Næss call complex (p. 463), are not described and are taken as unchanged.

name: Tanimbili
orthography_note: Ross & Næss write the prenasalised stops b, d, g and the RSC vowels as in the practical orthographies; reflexes here are in IPA, with source_form where they differ.
notes: Data from Tryon & Hackman (1983). Its reflexes of *t are analysed in Ross & Næss (2007: 470). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 2 gives the other consonants as the parent's; the vowels, which Ross & Næss call complex (p. 463), are not described and are taken as unchanged.

name: Proto-Nuclear Cenderawasih Bay
notes: Defined by three morphological innovations in subject marking: the 2sg infix *‹u›, the 3sg infix *‹i› and the 3sg vocalic conjugation prefix *dy- (Kamholz 2024: 184). Kamholz renamed his earlier Proto-Cenderawasih Bay to avoid confusion with the region (p. 183, n. 3). Members in Table 14.1: Proto-Biakic, Proto-Yapen, Proto-Southwest Cenderawasih Bay. No Glottocode: Glottolog's Cenderawasih Bay (cend1238) is not checked for the same membership.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Yapen
notes: Defined by the 2sg vocalic conjugation subject prefix *bu- (Kamholz 2024: 184). Glottocode yape1249 (Yapen).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Western Yapen
notes: Defined by innovations in inalienable possessive marking (3sg -mpai, 3sg -na/-ni, plural -mi/-mu) and the plural vocalic conjugation linking consonant *-t- (Kamholz 2024: 184). It contains Proto-Central Yapen (Table 14.1). Glottocode cent2277 (Central-Western Yapen).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Central Yapen
notes: Pom, Munggui, Papuma, Serui-Laut, Busami (Kamholz 2024: 183, Table 14.1). Glottocode cent2308 (Central Yapen).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Southwest Cenderawasih Bay
notes: Umar and Proto-Yaur-Yerisiam. Defined by PMP *z > Ø and an irregular *u > i in *punti 'banana', neither very secure, so tentative (Kamholz 2024: 184). *z > Ø is not a row: PSHWNG has already merged *z with *d as *l. Glottocode sout3230.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-South Halmahera
notes: Gebe, Proto-Central-Eastern and Proto-Southern South Halmahera. Defined by the 2pl subject prefix *f- and the 1pl.incl inalienable possessive suffix *-d (Kamholz 2024: 184). Glottocode sout3231.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Central-Eastern South Halmahera
notes: Buli, Maba, Patani, Sawai. Defined by a cross-paradigmatic innovation in inalienable possessive marking (Kamholz 2024: 184). Glottocode cent2270.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Kamholz defines the subgroup by morphological innovations only (2024: 183-184).

name: Proto-Malayo-Sumbawan
notes: Adelaar's (2005: 358, Figure 1) subgroup: Madurese, Sundanese and Proto-Malayo-Chamic-BSS (Malayic, Chamic and Balinese-Sasak-Sumbawa), excluding Javanese; it replaces the Malayo-Javanic subgroup of Nothofer (1975) and later work. The evidence is a configuration of phonological developments (Table 1, p. 360) and lexical items, not changes stated for the node itself. A proposed, not established node (decision adelaar2005-ms): its members stay under PMP and list it as a proposed parent. Not in Glottolog.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Adelaar states no change for the node itself.

name: Proto-Kayanic
notes: Smith's (2023: 327, 361-362) Kayanic: Kayan, Modang and Segai, with Murik-Merap (Smith 2017a). One of the seven Bornean subgroups that descend directly from PMP in his model (§7, Figure 6). Glottocode kaya1335 (Glottolog's Kayan-Murik-Modang, the same membership; Glottolog's 'Kayanic', kaya1333, is Proto-Kayan's). Smith (2017a: 86) finds no phonological evidence for Kayanic, so the node has no changes of its own; the shared changes stay on Proto-Kayan, Proto-Murik-Merap and Proto-Segai-Modang (decision kayanic-held). Entered on the user's instruction of 23 November 2026 (decision smith2023-nodes).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Smith (2023: 361-362) gives the subgroup without sound changes of its own.

name: Proto-Central Sarawak
notes: Smith's (2023: 327-328, 361-362) Central Sarawak: Melanau, Kajang, Punan and Upper-Kapuas-Mahakam (Müller-Schwaner). One of the seven Bornean subgroups in his model (§7, Figure 6). Glottocode sara1342 (Glottolog's Central Sarawak, Melanau-Kajang and Punan-Muller-Schwaner: the same membership). No changes of its own are stated. Entered on the user's instruction of 23 November 2026 (decision smith2023-nodes).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Smith (2023: 361-362) gives the subgroup without sound changes of its own.

name: Proto-Northeast Sabah
notes: Smith's (2023: 328, 361-362) Northeast Sabah: Idaanic and Bonggi (Blust 2010). One of the seven Bornean subgroups in his model (§7, Figure 6), no longer under North Borneo. Glottocode nort3172 (Glottolog's Northeast Sabahan: Ida'an and Bonggi). No changes of its own are stated. Entered on the user's instruction of 23 November 2026 (decision smith2023-nodes).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Smith (2023: 361-362) gives the subgroup without sound changes of its own.

name: Barito-Basap Linkage
region: Borneo; Malagasy and Sama-Bajaw outside it
notes: Smith's (2018; 2023: 327-328, 361-362) Barito-Basap linkage: the Barito languages (with Malagasy), Sama-Bajaw and the Basap varieties, the remnant of a dialect network from the Barito River to North Kalimantan; the eighth member of his Bornean model (§7, Figure 6). A linkage: a node of the tree with no proto-language, no rows and no page (decision smith2023-nodes). Glottocode basa1291 (Glottolog's Basap-Greater Barito, which includes Sama-Bajaw).

name: Proto-Loyalties
notes: Lynch (2003b): the ancestor of Iaai, Drehu and Nengone. It inherited PNC's geminate voiceless stops and made them aspirates; its bilabials were probably palatalised, fronting a following *a and *u (pp. 159, 164). Glottocode loya1239 (Glottolog's Loyalty Islands: the same three languages). Changes other than PNC *pp > *pʰ are not stated, so the rest of PNC is carried down (decision lynch2003b-ploy).
inherit_note: Not mentioned by Lynch (2003b), who states only the change of the geminates: retained from PNC.

name: V'ënen Taut
orthography_note: Lynch writes the linguolabials p', v', m' (here t̼, ð̼, n̼); v is the bilabial fricative β.
notes: Northwest Malakula. Lynch (2019a: 296-298, Table 1) states its labial reflexes against POc/PNCV from Crowley's list of about 700 words culled from Fox (1979), with Tryon (1976); Lynch & Brotchie (2010: 380, Table 3) give the same reflexes. Placed under POc with Southern Oceanic as its tree parent, as Nese and Naman are (decision lynch-parents): Lynch states the changes from POc. Royce Dodd (pers. comm. in Lynch 2019a: 299) reports younger speakers replacing the linguolabials, especially v', with bilabials.

name: Tirax
orthography_note: Brotchie's orthography: x velar fricative; v bilabial fricative β (Lynch 2019a: 294, n. 3); t, d, n, l dental, s and r alveolar.
notes: About 800 speakers on the northeast coast of Malakula; traditionally in the mountains of north central Malakula (Brotchie 2009: 1, in Lynch & Brotchie 2010: 379). Lynch & Brotchie state the reflexes from POc (with PNCV forms where these differ); placed under POc with Southern Oceanic as tree parent, as Nese is (decision lynch-parents). The apicolabial shift in Tirax followed low vowel deletion, which no other shifting language has, so they take the shift to be borrowed into Tirax (pp. 371-372, 385).

name: Malua-Tepërav
notes: Language node for the Malua Bay dialect (Glottolog).

name: Malua Bay
notes: Between V'ënen Taut and Nese on the north coast of Malakula; does not show the apicolabial shift. Data from Tryon (1976), via Lynch & Brotchie (2010: 380, Table 3).

name: Vovo
notes: Glottolog files Vovo as a dialect of Nese. Data from Tryon (1976), via Lynch & Brotchie (2010: 380, Table 3): the shift applies to *b and *m in a minority of etyma only, not to *p.

name: Botovro
notes: North Coast Malakula. Data from Tryon (1976), via Lynch & Brotchie (2010: 380, Table 3) and Lynch (2019a: 304, Table 4): mostly linguolabials, with some apicals.

name: Vao
region: Vao Island and the neighbouring north Malakula mainland, Vanuatu
notes: Glottolog's Vao-Vovo; the data are Vao (Tryon 1976, via Lynch & Brotchie 2010: 380, Table 3).

name: Rennellese
notes: Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from Ross et al. (2023: 623-629). Marck's Ren row (Table 2.2) is entered here and his Bel row on Bellona (decision ren-bel). Parent after Wilson (2021); Marck's (2000) parent, Proto-Nuclear Polynesian, is a proposed parent (decision pn-tree). Since 24 November 2026 the Rennellese dialect (Glottolog's Munggava, mung1271) of Rennell-Bellona; before, this lect had the language's id and code, renn1242.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Marck's Table 2.2 (pp. 23-24) gives the same consonant, and Table 3.1 (p. 74) no regular vowel change.

name: Paranan-Pahanan
notes: Robinson & Lobel (2013: 147-148, Figure 1) group Pahanan Agta with Paranan; no proto-language is reconstructed. Glottolog's Paranan-Pahanan (para1320). Their other pair, Casiguran with Nagtipunan ('very closely related, if not dialects of a single language'), is the language Casiguran-Nagtipunan Agta with Nagtipunan as its dialect; Dupaningan Agta is a primary branch and Dinapigue is unplaced (decision neluz-internal).

name: Toda-Truku
notes: Song (2025: 153-167) divides Seediq into Tgdaya and Toda-Truku, and Toda-Truku into Toda and Truku; no proto-language is reconstructed for the subgroups (decision song-seediq).

name: Toda

A group with no proto-language: the two changes are still stated on Punan Tubu and Punan Bah, and the backing of final *ə that these two share with Punan Aput and Beketan cuts across the group (pp. 120-122). name: Erakor

Glottolog has no code for it (decision sef-dialects). Spoken in Pango, Erakor and Eratap on the south coast of Efate; Eton, Pangpang and Epau speak divergent varieties, possibly transitional to Nakanamanga (Lynch 2000b: 320). Lynch's data are Erakor (Thieberger 1997, 1998, 2000); Eton and Epau only as reported by Clark (1985). Lynch argues that South Efate's dissimilation and vowel deletion rules, in the order of Southern Vanuatu, suggest that it subgroups with the Southern Vanuatu languages (pp. 332-337); entered under POc (decision lynch-parents). Glottocode, ISO code and coordinates from the language metadata of Ross et al. (2023: 628, 'S Efate').

name: Proto-Admiralty
notes: Lynch et al. (2002: 99): the Admiralties family is defined by, among others, POc *R > *y before high vowels and its loss elsewhere. Only that change is entered; the other phonemes are taken as retained from POc. Glottolog's Admiralty Islands (admi1239). Mussau (St Matthias) is not part of it (decision lrc2002-subgroups).

name: Tobian
region: Hatohobei (Tobi), Palau; now mostly Echang, Koror
orthography_note: IPA, with the inventory of van den Berg (2014: 14-23): ts = t͡ʃ, h = x, r = ɾ, y = j; bw and mw (her velarized [bˠ], [mˠ]) are written bʷ and mʷ as in the other Chuukic lects (decision vandenberg2014-symbols).
notes: South-West Islands of Palau. van den Berg (2014: 6-10) places Hatohobeian and Sonsorolese together as the westernmost group of the Chuukic continuum, closer to each other than to their eastern neighbours, and describes them together; Jackson's (1983) tree, which she cites, does not include them. name: Nguluwan
region: Ngulu Atoll, Yap State; also Guror village, Gilman', Yap
orthography_note: IPA, from Sakiyama's transcription (pp. 107-108), which differs from the official Yapese spelling in the long vowels (ëë for ea, ää for ae, öö for oe): ch = t͡ʃ, j = d͡ʒ, th = θ, ng = ŋ, y = j; ë [æ], ä [ɐ], ö [œ], a [ɑ]; doubled letters for long vowels (decision sakiyama1982-symbols).
notes: Spoken by 28 people on Ngulu Atoll and by some in Guror, Gilman', which holds Ngulu in a soway relationship (Sakiyama 1982: 105). 'Neither Yapese nor Ulithian in the strict sense of the word, although we can define it as a quite peculiar dialect among Yapese', with Ulithian loans and calques in the lexicon and in possessive constructions (pp. 106, 113); entered as a dialect of Yapese (decision sakiyama1982-nguluwan). Glottolog 5.4 has Nguluwan as a language beside Yapese in Yapic (yape1250). Sakiyama compares it with Yapese (§1.3, pp. 108-111): Nguluwan lacks all of Yapese's glottalized consonants and its glottal stop q; Yapese -iq is -iy, -oq is -wwa, medial q is w or y (naqun : nawun 'house', raqay : rayay 'hundred'); Yapese bVqV-, mVqV- are bwV-, mwV-; Yapese d and th merge as th; words begin with glides y-, w- where Yapese has a vowel (arow : yaraw 'land'); vowel correspondences are not regular. 'Such innovations are much indebted to Ulithian influence' (p. 111). No correspondence rows: the lect is shown by its sourced inventory. Coordinates from Glottolog.
